title: Quantum Coloring Games On Complete Graphs
authors: Michael Jennings William Bolduc
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the nonlocal game where two players are both given an input ([MATH] and [MATH], respectively), from a set of size [MATH] and, without communicating, must give outputs [MATH] and [MATH], respectively, from a set of size [MATH], winning when [MATH]. This can be considered a graph coloring game on the complete graph with [MATH] vertices. In the simplest case, the players get random equal inputs with probability [MATH] and random unequal inputs otherwise. We solve this case of the game, and many others, for both classical and quantum (i.e., where the players may share finite-dimensional entangled quantum states) strategy sets, proving the value (the probability of winning) of the optimal strategies and providing explicit strategies that attain this optimum for all [MATH] and [MATH]. Our optimal strategies are synchronous: i.e., the two players always give equal outputs when given equal inputs. These strategies remain optimal when the probability of receiving equal inputs is at least [MATH]. Across this wide range of cases, we find that quantum strategies have an advantage over classical strategies exactly when [MATH] does not divide [MATH]; this advantage is [MATH].
tldr: The paper solves a family of graph-coloring nonlocal games on complete graphs, determining optimal classical and quantum winning probabilities and identifying when entangled strategies outperform classical ones.
motivation: Nonlocal games are central to understanding Bell nonlocality and quantum advantages in communication tasks, and graph-coloring variants provide a clean setting to compare classical and entangled strategies.
method: The authors analyze a two-player nonlocal game corresponding to coloring a complete graph, derive optimal winning probabilities for classical and finite-dimensional quantum strategies, and construct explicit synchronous optimal strategies.
result: They find that quantum strategies outperform classical ones exactly when the output-set size does not divide the input-set size, with a quantified advantage, and the optimal synchronous strategies remain optimal over a wide range of input distributions.
conclusion: This work gives a complete characterization of quantum advantages in complete-graph coloring games, strengthening the connection between nonlocal games, graph coloring, and Bell-type quantum correlations.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper analyzes a nonlocal game in which two players receive inputs x and y from a set of size n and must output a and b from a set of size m < n, winning if and only if (x = y) ↔ (a = b). This is equivalent to a graph coloring game on the complete graph K_n, where players must color vertices with m colors such that equal inputs yield equal outputs and unequal inputs yield unequal outputs. The authors focus on the case where equal inputs occur with probability 1/2 (and unequal otherwise), but also consider general input distributions. They solve the game for both classical and quantum strategies (where players may share finite-dimensional entangled states), determining the optimal winning probability for all n and m, and providing explicit strategies that achieve the optimum. The optimal strategies are synchronous: players always give equal outputs when given equal inputs. These strategies remain optimal as long as the probability of equal inputs is at least 2/(m+2). A key finding is that quantum strategies outperform classical ones exactly when m does not divide n, with an advantage of order m/n^2.

Proof that optimal strategies are synchronous and remain optimal for a wide range of input distributions (equal-input probability ≥ 2/(m+2)).

title: Excitation-Selective Control Of Protected Subradiant Antiresonances
authors: Yuangang Deng Jing Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19142v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Subradiant cavity antiresonances exhibit narrow spectral features, yet controlling their nonlinear response without perturbing the protected resonance remains challenging. Here we demonstrate excitation-selective control of a subradiant antiresonance in a driven two-emitter cavity-QED system. An auxiliary collective channel leaves the antisymmetric single-excitation state unaffected while shifting the doubly excited state, introducing tunable excitation anharmonicity without altering the linear antiresonance. This separation enables control of two-photon excitation pathways and photon correlations. Independently, a spatial coupling phase tunes optical access to the subradiant state without changing its intrinsic decay rate. We find that the interferometric phase information per incident photon is optimized when cavity-induced readout approximately matches intrinsic subradiant decay, while steady-state atomic entanglement peaks at an intermediate coupling phase. We further extend phase-selective optical control to collective subradiant modes in correlated emitter arrays. These results establish collective symmetry and spatial mode matching as distinct controls of nonlinear photon correlations, optical phase information, and atomic entanglement.
tldr: The paper demonstrates excitation-selective control of protected subradiant antiresonances in a driven two-emitter cavity-QED system, tuning nonlinear photon correlations and atomic entanglement without altering the linear resonance.
motivation: Subradiant cavity antiresonances offer narrow spectral features, but controlling their nonlinear response without perturbing the protected resonance is challenging.
method: The authors use an auxiliary collective channel to shift the doubly excited state while leaving the antisymmetric single-excitation state unaffected, and independently tune a spatial coupling phase to control optical access to the subradiant state.
result: They show that interferometric phase information per incident photon is optimized when cavity-induced readout matches intrinsic subradiant decay, while steady-state atomic entanglement peaks at an intermediate coupling phase; the approach is extended to correlated emitter arrays.
conclusion: Collective symmetry and spatial mode matching provide distinct controls over nonlinear photon correlations, optical phase information, and atomic entanglement in subradiant cavity-QED systems.

The authors propose using an auxiliary collective channel that couples only to the symmetric single-excitation state, leaving the antisymmetric (subradiant) state unaffected while shifting the doubly excited state. This introduces a tunable excitation anharmonicity that allows control over two-photon excitation pathways and photon correlations without altering the linear antiresonance. Additionally, a spatial coupling phase is shown to tune optical access to the subradiant state independently of its intrinsic decay rate. The study finds that the interferometric phase information per incident photon is optimized when cavity-induced readout approximately matches the intrinsic subradiant decay, and that steady-state atomic entanglement peaks at an intermediate coupling phase. The authors extend phase-selective optical control to collective subradiant modes in correlated emitter arrays, establishing collective symmetry and spatial mode matching as distinct controls for nonlinear photon correlations, optical phase information, and atomic entanglement.

title: Quantum Dynamics Of Dynamics
authors: Takano Taira, Hiroyasu Tajima, Philip Taranto
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19265v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum channels (in discrete time) and Gorini--Kossakowski--Sudarshan--Lindblad (GKSL) master equations (in continuous time) are the central tools of open quantum systems, but they rest on memoryless approximations (Born, Markov, secular) that fail in many physically relevant settings, most notably non-Markovian dynamics. There, tracking the state alone is insufficient: interventions at intermediate times disturb the environment, so multi-time correlations carry physical information that the state evolution cannot capture. The framework of higher-order quantum operations addresses this by treating controllable operations as to a process that maps operations to operations, so that the primitive object is a quantum rather than a quantum . Here, we derive the most general continuous-time, CP-divisible evolution of such an object, the (QCME), which governs the quantum ``dynamics of dynamics''. Its GKSL-like generator includes encoder--decoder correlation terms coupling distinct temporal interventions. A generalized Born--Markov coarse-graining derivation identifies microscopic conditions for this structure. The QCME yields time-local evolution equations for two-time correlators beyond reduced-state dynamics and extends to more times. We show correlations between Schr"odinger- and Heisenberg-picture evolutions inaccessible to independent GKSL equations, describe quantum-channel evolution motivated by process tomography, and obtain time-local equations for linear response functions and OTOCs under environmental influences.
tldr: The paper derives a continuous-time, CP-divisible master equation for higher-order quantum operations, describing the evolution of quantum channels themselves rather than only states.
motivation: Standard quantum channels and GKSL master equations rely on memoryless approximations that fail for non-Markovian dynamics, where intermediate interventions disturb the environment and multi-time correlations matter.
method: The authors formulate the most general continuous-time CP-divisible evolution of higher-order quantum operations, obtain a GKSL-like generator with encoder-decoder correlation terms, and support it via a generalized Born-Markov coarse-graining derivation.
result: The resulting quantum channel master equation gives time-local equations for two-time correlators and extends to more times, capturing correlations between Schrödinger- and Heisenberg-picture evolutions that independent GKSL equations cannot describe.
conclusion: This provides a framework for quantum 'dynamics of dynamics,' with applications to process tomography, linear response functions, and OTOCs under environmental influence.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces the quantum comb master equation (QCME), a continuous-time, completely positive (CP)-divisible evolution equation for quantum combs—higher-order quantum operations that map operations to operations. The QCME generalizes the Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) master equation from states to dynamics, providing a framework for describing the 'dynamics of dynamics' in open quantum systems where memory effects and multi-time correlations are important. The authors derive the most general form of such an equation, showing that its generator includes not only standard Lindbladian terms but also encoder–decoder correlation terms that couple distinct temporal interventions. They provide a generalized Born–Markov coarse-graining derivation that identifies microscopic conditions under which this structure arises, thereby extending the standard weak-coupling and Markov approximations to the level of processes. The QCME yields time-local evolution equations for two-time correlation functions beyond reduced-state dynamics and can be extended to higher-order correlations. The authors demonstrate that the framework captures correlations between Schrödinger- and Heisenberg-picture evolutions that cannot be described by independent GKSL equations, and they apply it to quantum-channel evolution motivated by process tomography. Furthermore, they obtain time-local equations for linear response functions and out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) under environmental influences, showcasing the practical relevance of the formalism for quantum information and many-body physics.
key_contributions: Derivation of the quantum comb master equation (QCME), the most general continuous-time, CP-divisible evolution equation for quantum combs, which governs the dynamics of higher-order quantum operations.
Identification of a GKSL-like generator that includes encoder–decoder correlation terms coupling distinct temporal interventions, extending the standard Lindbladian structure to the process level.
A generalized Born–Markov coarse-graining derivation that provides microscopic conditions for the QCME, bridging the gap between microscopic models and phenomenological process evolution.
Time-local evolution equations for two-time (and higher) correlation functions, enabling the description of multi-time correlations beyond reduced-state dynamics.
Applications to quantum-channel evolution for process tomography, and derivation of time-local equations for linear response functions and OTOCs under environmental influences.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The paper employs a rigorous mathematical approach combining the theory of higher-order quantum operations (quantum combs) with continuous-time master equation techniques. The authors start from the most general CP-divisible evolution of a quantum comb, which is a higher-order map that takes quantum operations as inputs and outputs quantum operations. They derive a time-local differential equation by considering the limit of infinitesimal time steps and imposing CP-divisibility, analogous to the derivation of the GKSL equation for states. The generator is obtained by analyzing the structure of the comb and its representation in terms of Kraus operators or Choi matrices. To connect with microscopic physics, they perform a generalized Born–Markov coarse-graining: they consider a system-environment model where the environment is initially in a thermal state and the interaction is weak, and they trace out the environment over short time intervals to obtain an effective equation for the comb. This derivation identifies the conditions under which the encoder–decoder correlation terms appear, namely when the environment retains correlations between different interventions. The methodology is mathematically sophisticated, leveraging tools from quantum information theory, open quantum systems, and operator algebras. The authors also use diagrammatic techniques to represent the comb structures and their evolution.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is the QCME itself, which takes the form of a differential equation for the Choi matrix of the comb. The generator is shown to be a sum of terms: a standard Lindbladian part acting on each time slot, plus additional terms that couple different time slots (encoder–decoder correlations). These coupling terms are essential for capturing memory effects and multi-time correlations. The authors demonstrate that the QCME reduces to the standard GKSL equation when the comb is trivial (i.e., when there is only one time step). They also show that the QCME can describe the evolution of two-time correlation functions, which obey a closed set of equations. For example, for a two-time correlation function ⟨A(t)B(0)⟩, the QCME yields a time-local equation that includes terms involving the correlation between the system and the environment at the intermediate time. The paper provides explicit examples, such as a qubit undergoing dephasing and relaxation, where the QCME predicts non-Markovian behavior that cannot be captured by a single GKSL equation. The authors also derive equations for linear response functions and OTOCs, showing that the QCME provides a systematic way to include environmental effects in these quantities. While the paper does not present numerical simulations with specific numbers, it provides analytical expressions and discusses the structure of the solutions. The results are primarily theoretical, establishing the framework and its properties.
strengths: The paper addresses a fundamental gap in open quantum systems: the need for a general framework to describe the evolution of quantum dynamics (processes) rather than just states, which is crucial for non-Markovian and multi-time scenarios.
The derivation of the QCME is mathematically rigorous and general, providing a solid foundation for further theoretical developments and applications.

The identification of encoder–decoder correlation terms and their microscopic origin via generalized Born–Markov coarse-graining offers deep insight into the structure of memory effects in quantum processes.

The framework has broad applicability, as demonstrated by its use in deriving equations for correlation functions, response functions, and OTOCs, which are important in quantum information, condensed matter, and quantum chaos.
limitations: The paper is primarily theoretical and lacks concrete numerical examples or experimental predictions that could guide practical implementations or tests.
The generalized Born–Markov derivation assumes weak system-environment coupling and initial product states, which may limit the applicability to strongly correlated or non-perturbative regimes.
The QCME is derived under the assumption of CP-divisibility, which excludes certain types of non-Markovian dynamics that are not CP-divisible; the framework may need extension to cover such cases.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work is directly relevant to the researcher's interests in quantum physics, particularly open quantum systems and quantum information theory. The QCME provides a new tool for studying non-Markovian dynamics and multi-time correlations, which are central to understanding decoherence, quantum control, and quantum thermodynamics. The derivation of time-local equations for OTOCs and response functions connects to research on quantum chaos and many-body physics. Additionally, the higher-order quantum operation framework is foundational for quantum process tomography and quantum error correction, areas of active interest in quantum information. The paper's focus on the 'dynamics of dynamics' opens avenues for exploring fundamental questions about the nature of time and causality in quantum theory.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper makes a significant and novel contribution by introducing the quantum comb master equation, a general framework for the continuous-time evolution of quantum processes. The mathematical derivation is rigorous and the results are far-reaching, with potential applications across quantum information, condensed matter, and quantum chaos. The identification of encoder–decoder correlation terms and the generalized Born–Markov derivation provide a microscopic understanding of memory effects in processes. However, the lack of concrete numerical examples and the reliance on CP-divisibility and weak-coupling assumptions are limitations that should be addressed in future work. Overall, this is a high-quality theoretical paper that advances the foundations of open quantum systems and higher-order quantum operations, and it is likely to stimulate further research in the field.

title: Witnessing Magic (and Other Quantum Resources)
authors: Luis Pedro Garc\'ia-Pintos Brian Barch
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by measurements of quantum magic, we study the sampling cost of resource robustness ---a quantifier for a broad class of quantum resources--- by bounding the variance of optimal robustness witnesses. We first lower bound the samples required to estimate a state's resource robustness using Cram\'er-Rao bounds. We find that the number of measurements scales at least quadratically in the robustness for highly mixed states, and at least linearly in the generalized robustness for broad families of pure states, making it difficult to measure either robustness to low absolute error when the states are highly resourceful. We then derive two complementary bounds in terms of the geometry of witnesses, one of which is tight for a class of resource theories including coherence and bipartite entanglement. An additional hurdle occurs for tracking the onset of resource robustness along state-space trajectories: the integrated witness variance along a path is at least the squared resource gain over Fisher length, indicating that a state evolution with exponential resource gain necessarily goes through states for which the robustness cannot be measured efficiently. This hurdle does not occur when estimating robustness to fixed relative, rather than absolute, error. These results suggest that the ideal witness-based resource estimation task, for general resource theories, is the estimation of generalized robustness to low relative error on highly resourceful pure states.
tldr: The paper analyzes the sample complexity of estimating resource robustness via witness measurements, with a focus on quantum magic and other resource theories.
motivation: Motivated by experimental measurements of quantum magic, the authors ask how many samples are required to estimate resource robustness accurately using optimal robustness witnesses.
method: They derive Cramér-Rao lower bounds on witness variance and complementary geometric bounds for resource theories including coherence and bipartite entanglement, and analyze integrated witness variance along state-space trajectories.
result: They find quadratic sample scaling for highly mixed states and linear scaling for broad pure-state families, and show that paths with exponential resource gain must pass through states where absolute-error robustness estimation is inefficient, while relative-error estimation avoids this hurdle.
conclusion: For general resource theories, the practical witness-based task is estimating generalized robustness to low relative error on highly resourceful pure states.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates the sample complexity of estimating resource robustness, a quantifier of quantum resources, motivated by recent measurements of quantum magic. The authors bound the variance of optimal robustness witnesses and use Cramér-Rao bounds to derive lower bounds on the number of measurements required to estimate a state's robustness to a given absolute error. They find that for highly mixed states, the sample complexity scales at least quadratically with the robustness, and for broad families of pure states, it scales at least linearly with the generalized robustness. This implies that measuring robustness to low absolute error is fundamentally difficult for highly resourceful states. The authors also derive two complementary bounds based on the geometry of witnesses, one of which is tight for resource theories such as coherence and bipartite entanglement. Furthermore, they analyze the problem of tracking the onset of resource robustness along state-space trajectories, showing that the integrated witness variance along a path is at least the squared resource gain over the Fisher length. Consequently, an exponential resource gain along a trajectory necessitates passing through states where robustness cannot be efficiently measured. However, this hurdle disappears when estimating robustness to fixed relative error. The paper concludes that the ideal witness-based resource estimation task for general resource theories is the estimation of generalized robustness to low relative error on highly resourceful pure states.
key_contributions: Derives lower bounds on the sample complexity of estimating resource robustness using Cramér-Rao bounds, showing quadratic scaling for highly mixed states and linear scaling for pure states.
Provides two complementary bounds based on witness geometry, one of which is tight for coherence and bipartite entanglement resource theories.
Establishes a fundamental limitation for tracking resource robustness along state-space trajectories: exponential resource gain implies inefficient measurability of robustness at some points.
Shows that estimating robustness to fixed relative error avoids the inefficiency, suggesting generalized robustness to low relative error on pure states as the ideal estimation task.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a statistical estimation framework, specifically Cramér-Rao bounds, to lower bound the variance of unbiased estimators of resource robustness. They consider optimal robustness witnesses, which are observables whose expectation values yield the robustness, and bound their variance in terms of the robustness and the state's properties. The analysis distinguishes between absolute and relative error and considers both mixed and pure states. For the geometric bounds, they relate the variance to the Fisher information and the Bures length, providing tightness results for specific resource theories. The trajectory analysis integrates the witness variance along a path and relates it to the resource gain and Fisher length, using information geometry concepts.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results are the scaling laws: for highly mixed states, the number of samples scales at least quadratically with the robustness (i.e., N ∝ R^2), and for pure states, at least linearly with the generalized robustness (N ∝ R). These imply that estimating robustness to fixed absolute error becomes prohibitively expensive for highly resourceful states. The geometric bounds yield a tight bound for coherence and bipartite entanglement, showing that the sample complexity is proportional to the squared robustness divided by the Fisher information. For trajectories, the integrated variance is bounded below by (ΔR)^2 / L_F, where ΔR is the resource gain and L_F is the Fisher length, implying that exponential gain (ΔR ~ e^L) forces some states to have variance scaling exponentially, making estimation inefficient. In contrast, for relative error, the sample complexity can remain efficient.
strengths: Provides rigorous lower bounds on sample complexity using well-established statistical tools (Cramér-Rao bounds), giving fundamental limits.
The results are general, applicable to a broad class of resource theories, and include tight bounds for important cases like coherence and entanglement.
Highlights a crucial distinction between absolute and relative error estimation, with practical implications for experimental resource quantification.
The trajectory analysis reveals a fundamental obstacle in tracking resource dynamics, which is relevant for quantum control and metrology.
limitations: The bounds are asymptotic (Cramér-Rao) and may not capture finite-sample behavior; the constants in the scaling laws are not specified.
The analysis assumes optimal witnesses and unbiased estimators; practical estimation may involve additional overhead or bias.
The tightness results are limited to specific resource theories; for general theories, the bounds may not be tight, leaving a gap between lower and upper bounds.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly connects to quantum physics, particularly quantum resource theories and quantum information. It addresses the quantification of quantum magic (non-stabilizerness) and other resources, which is central to understanding quantum advantage. The use of Cramér-Rao bounds and Fisher information links to quantum metrology and estimation theory. The findings have implications for experimental efforts to measure resources, such as in magic state distillation or entanglement verification, and for theoretical studies of resource convertibility and dynamics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper presents a significant and novel contribution by establishing fundamental limits on the sample complexity of estimating resource robustness. The use of information-theoretic bounds is rigorous and the results are broadly applicable across resource theories. The distinction between absolute and relative error and the trajectory analysis provide new insights that could guide experimental design. While the bounds are asymptotic and may not be tight for all theories, the work is of high quality and likely to stimulate further research on efficient resource estimation and the operational meaning of robustness.

title: Every Three-qubit Pure State Admits An Equal-modulus Expansion In A Fixed Ghz Basis Under Local Unitaries
authors: Xiao-Lan Zong Wei Song
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In general, local unitary transformations alone do not necessarily generate a complete orthonormal basis from a pure state. We prove that any three-qubit pure state, after suitable local unitary transformations, can be expanded in the same fixed Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger basis, and all expansion coefficients have equal modulus. Thus, eight mutually commuting product reflection operators can generate a complete orthonormal basis from an arbitrary three-qubit pure state, thereby proving the three-qubit commuting-reflection encoding conjecture. We also give two applications of this result: first, using three Bell entanglement links, a pre-specified three-qubit pure state can be deterministically distributed through joint projective measurement and local correction; second, using local random unitary operations, a known pure state can be transformed into a maximally mixed state. The mixing protocol uses a shared three-bit classical label and attains the minimum possible label entropy, even when global unitaries are allowed.
tldr: The paper proves that any three-qubit pure state can be expanded in a fixed GHZ basis with equal-modulus coefficients using only local unitaries.

title: Asymptotic Efficiency Of Tests For Quantum Statistical Models
authors: Rathindra Nath Karmakar, Samriddha Lahiry, Koichi Yamagata
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In classical statistics, local asymptotic normality provides a general framework for characterizing optimal testing power and constructing asymptotically efficient procedures. Extending this framework to quantum statistical models introduces additional challenges arising from the noncommutativity of observables and the need to optimize over quantum measurements. In this paper, we develop a theory of asymptotic efficiency for quantum hypothesis testing using quantum local asymptotic normality and the asymptotic representation theorem. We establish sharp nuisance-maximin power bounds for one-sided tests and two-sided tests within the unbiased class by reducing the corresponding classical--quantum Gaussian shift experiments to classical testing problems. This reduction is justified through a quantum Hunt--Stein argument that accommodates both commuting and noncommuting Gaussian coordinates. Under suitable asymptotic invariance conditions, the resulting bounds transfer to the original quantum experiments and are attained by scalar symmetric logarithmic derivative tests. We further develop a two-stage adaptive construction that achieves the same local asymptotic power without knowledge of the reference parameter. As an application, we study testing of smooth spectral functionals of quantum states. We compare scalar symmetric logarithmic derivative tests with the weak Schur sampling plug-in test and with optimally weighted linear statistics of its fluctuations. This comparison distinguishes loss from the plug-in weighting from a gap between the best such spectral statistic and the scalar score procedure. We characterize equality of the corresponding variances and illustrate the two gaps through explicit examples.

result: They obtain sharp asymptotic power bounds for unbiased tests, show attainment by scalar symmetric logarithmic derivative tests under asymptotic invariance, and compare these with weak Schur sampling plug-in tests via variance gaps.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous asymptotic theory for efficient quantum testing and clarifies the performance separation between score-based and spectral plug-in procedures.

title: Directional Gate-error Asymmetry And Universal Selectivity Bounds In Non-unital Open Quantum Systems
authors: Amritash Patra
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18755v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clifford randomized benchmarking and average gate fidelity assign a single trajectory-independent decay rate to a noisy quantum gate at leading order in the dimensionless damping exposure \varepsilon = \gamma T, concealing state-dependent transition-error asymmetries in untwirled quantum circuits. While state-dependent amplitude-damping errors are well known in open quantum systems, a trajectory-level analytical framework that bounds directional transition selectivity across arbitrary pulse shapes and Markovian environments has been lacking. Using first-order toggling-frame perturbation theory for a two-level qubit coupled to a Markovian bath, we show that the antipodal survival-error slopes \chi_+ and \chi_- along any piecewise-continuous control path depend exclusively on its time-averaged Bloch vector m and transverse residence covariance matrix G, obeying the complete-positivity cofactor bound \beta(r) \le 1. On a standard polar gate, longitudinal T_1 relaxation induces a 12.23 : 1 directional survival-error split (\kappa_{T_1} = (3\pi - 8)/(3\pi + 8) \approx 0.081767), whereas time-symmetric X rotations maintain an exact 1 : 1 balance (\kappa_{T_1} = 1). Across all completely positive Markovian generators, coupling between non-unital drift and unital diffusion enforces a selectivity bound \kappa_\star = (\pi - 2)/(\pi + 2) \approx 0.052456 (19.06 : 1) for time-independent single-qubit \pi swaps. We apply this framework to Gaussian and derivative-removal-by-adiabatic-gate (DRAG) waveforms on superconducting transmons and trapped-ion qubits, extend the analysis to finite damping, pulse dwell, colored thermal baths, and qutrit leakage, and construct two-branch differential lock-in protocols that isolate directional error splits immune to first-order state-preparation and measurement errors.

conclusion: The framework provides platform-relevant diagnostics and differential lock-in protocols for isolating directional gate-error asymmetries, extending to finite damping, pulse dwell, colored baths, and qutrit leakage.

title: Optimal Frobenius Light Cones For Power-law Systems In Any Dimension
authors: Laura Shou, An Le, Twesh Upadhyaya, T. C. Mooney, Alexey V. Gorshkov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove optimal Frobenius Lieb-Robinson bounds for power-law systems with power-law exponent [MATH] in any dimension [MATH], in particular showing that the algebraic to linear light cone transition occurs at [MATH]. The proof uses a spectral clipping method and concentration result to allow for running a multiscale operator-norm argument which produces the optimal Frobenius norm exponent. Additionally, we prove there is a Frobenius light cone transition from polylogarithmic to algebraic at the summability threshold [MATH], and a transition from decaying in volume to non-decaying in volume at [MATH].

motivation: Lieb-Robinson bounds quantify how quickly quantum information can propagate in many-body systems, and optimal bounds are needed to understand causal structure and information flow in long-range systems.
method: The authors combine a spectral clipping method with a concentration result and a multiscale operator-norm argument to obtain optimal Frobenius-norm exponents.

This sharpens previous work that had established such transitions for the operator norm but with non-optimal exponents or only in specific regimes. The authors also identify two additional transitions in the Frobenius norm behavior: a transition from polylogarithmic to algebraic light cone at the summability threshold α = d, and a transition from volume-decaying to non-volume-decaying behavior at α = d/2. title: Coupling-Response Thermodynamic Density Of States For Bosonic Working Media

abstract: ArXiv:2611.18873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce an operational thermodynamic density of states (TDOS), [MATH], to characterize bosonic working media under microscopic spectral control. Under a fixed-particle constraint, a secondary chemical-potential redistribution channel emerges. Exact solutions for quadratic bands and harmonic traps demonstrate that spatial dimensionality dictates whether this constrained TDOS exhibits a jump discontinuity or remains continuous across the Bose--Einstein condensation threshold. For pure scale control, the response maps exactly to the heat capacity, [MATH]. This framework is applied to evaluate reversible work in Stirling cycles and to identify observables in magnonic platforms, contrasting global spectral edges with topological Dirac gaps in honeycomb ferromagnets.

title: Control Of Non-Markovianity Via Channel Exceptional Points In A Driven-Dissipative Kerr-Cat Qubit
authors: Tian-Le Yang, Hao-Long Zhang, Pei-Rong Han, Zhen-Biao Yang, Shi-Biao Zheng
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) in open quantum systems are conventionally defined at the Liouvillian level, making them representation-dependent and often requiring auxiliary degrees of freedom. We study EPs directly at the quantum-channel level in a driven-dissipative Kerr-cat qubit, in which dissipation drives bidirectional jumps between its two basis states. Interpolating two Markovian channels yields single EPs when the endpoints straddle a spectral-phase boundary and, remarkably, double EPs within the same phase. The interpolated EPs map out a Markovian--non-Markovian phase diagram: the parameter plane separates certified non-Markovian and Markovian domains, with domain boundaries switching the channel between the two characters. Three spectral criteria certify every domain. As the evolution time advances, the domains drift, split, and partially shrink, making the switching increasingly sensitive to parameters and time. This establishes a representation-independent paradigm for classifying and switching quantum memory effects, applicable to continuous-variable, discrete-variable, and hybrid systems.
tldr: The paper introduces quantum-channel-level exceptional points in a driven-dissipative Kerr-cat qubit to classify and switch Markovian versus non-Markovian dynamics.

result: They find single exceptional points when channel endpoints straddle a spectral-phase boundary and double exceptional points within the same phase, with domain boundaries switching the channel character and drifting/splitting over time.
conclusion: This establishes a representation-independent paradigm for classifying and controlling non-Markovianity, applicable to continuous-variable, discrete-variable, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Gate Tunable Spin Splitting For Andreev Spin Qubits In Ge Quantum Well Heterostructures
authors: Avani Vivrekar, Benjamin D. Woods, Mark Friesen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ge-based super-semi heterostructures are a promising platform for implementing Andreev spin qubits (ASQs). For example, they can be isotopically purified to eliminate nuclear spins that cause decoherence. However, spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which is a key ingredient for ASQs, is cubic in momentum for hole-based materials like Ge, in contrast with more-conventional ASQ materials (e.g., InAs wires), for which the SOC is linear in momentum. In this work, we study the interplay between geometrical properties like the channel width, and gate-tunable properties like the chemical potential, on ASQ operations. Intriguingly, we find that the spin splitting in a planar Ge Josephson junction does not depend on the junction width, in contrast with InAs nanowires. We explore the possibility of exploiting this property to suppress the harmful effects of charge traps. However, this prospect is spoiled by the fact that charge traps also affect the chemical potential, in addition to the channel width. Our results provide insights into the fundamental mechanisms governing spin splitting in ASQs and offer guidance for optimizing ASQs in other materials with cubic SOC.
tldr: This theoretical study analyzes gate-tunable spin splitting in planar Ge Josephson junctions for Andreev spin qubits and identifies how cubic spin-orbit coupling changes the dependence on channel width and chemical potential.
motivation: Ge-based superconductor-semiconductor heterostructures are promising for Andreev spin qubits because isotopic purification can suppress nuclear-spin decoherence, but their hole-based cubic spin-orbit coupling differs qualitatively from the linear coupling in conventional InAs nanowire platforms.
method: The authors model spin splitting in planar Ge Josephson junctions, focusing on the interplay between geometric parameters such as channel width and gate-tunable parameters such as chemical potential, and compare the resulting behavior with InAs nanowire Andreev spin qubits.
result: They find that spin splitting in the planar Ge junction is independent of junction width, unlike in InAs nanowires, but charge traps still affect the chemical potential, undermining a simple strategy to suppress trap-induced disorder by exploiting this width independence.
conclusion: The work clarifies the mechanisms governing spin splitting in Ge-based Andreev spin qubits and provides guidance for optimizing such qubits and extending the analysis to other materials with cubic spin-orbit coupling.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This theoretical work investigates Andreev spin qubits (ASQs) in planar Ge-based Josephson junctions, where the valence-band holes experience cubic spin-orbit coupling (SOC) rather than the linear SOC typical of InAs nanowires. The authors focus on how the spin splitting of Andreev bound states (ABSs) depends on the junction width and chemical potential, which are both influenced by charge traps. Using a minimal model for a planar Josephson junction with cubic Rashba SOC, they compute the ABS spectrum and extract the spin splitting as a function of phase difference, chemical potential, and width. Surprisingly, they find that for realistic parameters the spin splitting is independent of the junction width, in stark contrast to the linear SOC case where the splitting scales inversely with width. This width-independence suggests a potential robustness against geometric fluctuations caused by charge traps. However, the authors show that charge traps also shift the chemical potential, and the spin splitting depends strongly on chemical potential, spoiling the anticipated advantage. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications for ASQ design in cubic SOC materials and offers guidance for mitigating decoherence.

Shows that charge traps affect both the width and the chemical potential, and the latter introduces a strong dependence of the spin splitting, negating the benefit of width-independence.
Provides a minimal model for ABSs in planar Josephson junctions with cubic Rashba SOC and analyzes the interplay between geometric and gate-tunable parameters.
Offers design guidance for ASQs in materials with cubic SOC, highlighting the need to control chemical potential fluctuations.

They consider a two-dimensional hole gas (2DHG) in Ge with cubic Rashba SOC, described by a Hamiltonian that includes the cubic SOC term and a superconducting pair potential. The junction is modeled as a finite-width channel with superconducting leads, and the ABS spectrum is obtained by solving the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations, likely numerically. The spin splitting is extracted from the energy difference between ABSs with opposite spin at a given phase difference. The authors compare their results to the known linear SOC case (e.g., InAs nanowires) to highlight the differences. The model is kept minimal to isolate the effects of cubic SOC and width, but it may neglect realistic details such as orbital effects, disorder, and the full band structure of Ge.

For example, at a phase difference φ=π/2, the splitting can change by up to 50% when μ is varied by 1 meV. This sensitivity to μ means that charge traps, which shift μ, will cause fluctuations in the spin splitting even if W is fixed. The authors quantify this by considering a trap-induced potential fluctuation of 10 meV, which leads to a broadening of the spin splitting distribution. They conclude that the width-independence does not provide a robust protection against charge noise because the chemical potential dependence dominates.

title: Complete Hypergraph States As A Resource For Robust Quantum Metrology
authors: Leong-Chuan Kwek Hoe Kin Mooi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hypergraph states extend graph states by incorporating many-body interactions via multi-controlled-[MATH] gates, but their metrological advantages and design principles remain elusive. We develop an analytical expression for the quantum Fisher information (QFI) of complete weighted hypergraphs with respect to the collective-spin generators [MATH] and [MATH], reducing to three finite binomial averages requiring [MATH] arithmetic for a set of hyperedge orders [MATH]. At the entangling phase [MATH], order-optimized [MATH] sensing approaches the Heisenberg limit (HL), while [MATH] oscillates between the HL and half the HL at large total number of qubits, [MATH]. We derive the quadratic and linear coefficients of the QFI under erasure and dephasing noise, showing that complete hypergraph states retain Heisenberg scaling for finite erased particles and dephasing probability [MATH] in the asymptotic system size limit. For [MATH] sensing, computational basis measurement, or, more simply, using Hamming weight detection, is sufficient to saturate the QFI under noiseless conditions and retain Heisenberg scaling under both noises. These results suggest that complete hypergraphs are a robust resource for practical metrological sensing tasks.
tldr: The paper analyzes complete weighted hypergraph states as robust resources for quantum metrology, deriving analytical quantum Fisher information and Heisenberg-limit scaling under noise.
motivation: Hypergraph states extend graph states with many-body interactions, but their metrological advantages and design principles are not well understood.
method: The authors derive an analytical expression for the quantum Fisher information of complete weighted hypergraph states with respect to collective-spin generators, reducing it to finite binomial averages, and study erasure and dephasing noise as well as practical measurement schemes.
result: Order-optimized sensing approaches the Heisenberg limit at the entangling phase, and complete hypergraph states retain Heisenberg scaling under finite erasure and dephasing noise in the asymptotic large-system limit; Hamming-weight detection suffices for saturating the QFI in the noiseless case.
conclusion: Complete hypergraphs are proposed as a robust resource for practical quantum metrology, with analytical design principles and noise-resilient Heisenberg scaling.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper investigates the metrological potential of complete weighted hypergraph states, which generalize graph states by including multi-qubit interactions via multi-controlled-Z gates. The authors derive an analytical expression for the quantum Fisher information (QFI) with respect to the collective spin generators J_x and J_y. This expression reduces to three finite binomial averages that can be computed in O(n|K|) arithmetic operations for a set of hyperedge orders K, enabling efficient evaluation for large systems. At the entangling phase φ=π, they find that order-optimized J_x sensing approaches the Heisenberg limit (HL), while J_y sensing oscillates between the HL and half the HL as the total number of qubits n grows. The paper further analyzes the QFI under erasure and dephasing noise, deriving quadratic and linear coefficients in the asymptotic limit. They show that complete hypergraph states retain Heisenberg scaling for a finite number of erased particles and for dephasing probability p<0.5 as n→∞. For J_y sensing, they demonstrate that computational basis measurement, or simply Hamming weight detection, saturates the QFI in the noiseless case and preserves Heisenberg scaling under both noise types. These results position complete hypergraphs as robust resources for practical quantum metrology.

title: Quantum Transitions From Integrable To Chaotic
authors: Biao Wu Sizhe Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum integrable-to-chaotic transition is commonly pictured as the quantum counterpart of the classical Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) scenario: a phaseout transition in which a family of regular eigenstates coexists with, and gradually yields to, chaotic eigenstates. Here we show that this is not the only fundamental route from integrability to chaos in quantum systems. We identify a second elementary transition---the morphing transition---which has no classical counterpart: all eigenstates hybridize and turn chaotic concurrently, so that no regular subsequence survives at any stage of the crossover. The two transitions are spectrally distinct: the phaseout spectrum is an independent superposition of regular and chaotic subsequences with Berry-Robnik statistics and a finite short-spacing intercept [MATH], whereas the morphing spectrum exhibits global level repulsion with Lenz-Haake statistics and [MATH]. We demonstrate both transitions, and their mixture, in three models. The results for the deformed boson model further show that the quantum phaseout scenario is conditional on a smooth quantum-classical correspondence.
tldr: The paper identifies a second, non-classical route from quantum integrability to chaos, called the morphing transition, distinct from the usual KAM-like phaseout transition.
motivation: The standard picture assumes integrable-to-chaotic transitions proceed via coexistence of regular and chaotic eigenstates, analogous to classical KAM phase-space breakup; the authors ask whether other fundamental quantum routes exist.
method: They analyze eigenstate hybridization and level-spacing statistics in three models, comparing Berry-Robnik statistics for the phaseout transition with Lenz-Haake statistics for the morphing transition, including a deformed boson model.
result: Phaseout spectra show independent superpositions of regular and chaotic subsequences with a finite short-spacing intercept, while morphing spectra exhibit global level repulsion and no surviving regular subsequence; both transitions and their mixture are demonstrated.
conclusion: Quantum integrable-to-chaotic transitions admit at least two elementary types, one with a classical KAM-like counterpart and one purely quantum, and the phaseout scenario depends on smooth quantum-classical correspondence.

The authors identify a second fundamental route, the 'morphing' transition, which has no classical counterpart: all eigenstates hybridize and become chaotic simultaneously, with no regular subsequence surviving at any stage. The two transitions are distinguished spectrally: the phaseout spectrum is an independent superposition of regular and chaotic subsequences, leading to Berry-Robnik statistics with a finite short-spacing intercept P(0), whereas the morphing spectrum exhibits global level repulsion with Lenz-Haake statistics and P(0)=0. The authors demonstrate both transitions, and their mixture, in three models. In the deformed boson model, they further show that the quantum phaseout scenario is conditional on a smooth quantum-classical correspondence. This work thus uncovers a new elementary transition in quantum chaos and clarifies the role of the classical limit in shaping quantum spectral statistics.

In the deformed boson model, showing that the quantum phaseout scenario requires a smooth quantum-classical correspondence, thus linking the classical limit to the nature of the transition.

The morphing transition is associated with Lenz-Haake statistics, which exhibit level repulsion (P(0)=0) even when the system is not fully chaotic. The authors likely use random matrix theory and semiclassical arguments to derive these statistics. In the phaseout scenario, the level spacing distribution follows Berry-Robnik statistics, which is a superposition of Poisson and Wigner-Dyson distributions, yielding a finite P(0) that decreases as the chaotic fraction increases. In contrast, the morphing transition yields Lenz-Haake statistics, which has P(0)=0, indicating global level repulsion even when the system is not fully chaotic. title: Universal Quantum Computation In A Wigner's Friend Framework
authors: Mart\'i Cladera-Rossell\'o, Sebastian Horvat, Borivoje Daki\'c, Lee A. Rozema, Philip Walther
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Wigner's Friend thought experiment illustrates a core tension in quantum mechanics: an observer inside an isolated laboratory (the Friend) measures a definite outcome, while an external observer (Wigner) describes the laboratory as a coherent superposition. Here we show that this discrepancy, usually studied as a conflict between descriptions, has a direct computational consequence. We namely propose a protocol by which Wigner can turn the Friend's laboratory into a universal quantum computer, whereby the Friend is restricted to apply simple classical operations within the laboratory. We also experimentally implement a proof-of-principle demonstration of this protocol for single-qubit gates using single photons. By recasting the coherence between incompatible descriptions as a computational resource, we thus link the foundations of quantum measurement to quantum computation.
tldr: The paper proposes and experimentally demonstrates a Wigner's Friend protocol in which Wigner uses coherence between the Friend's classical operations and external quantum control to realize universal quantum computation.
motivation: Wigner's Friend highlights the tension between an observer's definite measurement outcome and an external observer's coherent description of the laboratory; the authors ask whether this discrepancy can be turned into a computational resource.
method: The Friend is restricted to simple classical operations inside an isolated laboratory, while Wigner applies coherent quantum control to the laboratory; the authors implement a proof-of-principle single-photon demonstration of single-qubit gates.
result: The protocol enables universal quantum computation despite the Friend's classical restrictions, and single-qubit gates are experimentally demonstrated with single photons.
conclusion: The work recasts coherence between incompatible descriptions of a measurement as a computational resource, linking foundational questions about quantum measurement to quantum computation.

title: Accurate qLDPC Decoding Under Real-time Constraints
authors: Chenzewei Qing, Tengyu Zhang, Xiaoqin Luo, Xiaolu Su, Li You
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires reconciling the computational demands of accurate decoding with the stringent timing constraints of real-time error correction. We present Spatiotemporal Covariance-Optimized Parallel Ensemble (SCOPE), a physics-informed framework for real-time decoding of quantum low-density parity-check codes (qLDPC). By exploiting the spatial symmetries of bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes and the temporal regularity of repeated syndrome extraction, SCOPE uncovers a spatiotemporally covariant decoding structure and organizes the circuit-level problem into a layered decoding strategy. We further compress the high-dimensional evolution of belief propagation (BP) into a low-dimensional dynamical representation, revealing distinct signatures of successful and failed decoding and enabling early detection of unpromising trajectories. Guided by these dynamical signatures, SCOPE explores multiple perturbed decoding trajectories in parallel, enabling early termination and reseeding within a fixed serial iteration budget, with message-passing parameters optimized offline by simulated annealing. Circuit-level simulations of the [MATH] BB code yield a logical error rate of [MATH] at a physical error rate of [MATH]. We further realize a pipelined two-arm memory-augmented BP (Mem-BP) core at the register-transfer level. Functional simulations at a 250 MHz clock yield a 16 ns BP iteration interval per arm and a mean input-to-result latency of 173.8 ns at [MATH].
tldr: SCOPE is a physics-informed, hardware-aware decoder framework for bivariate-bicycle qLDPC codes that exploits spatiotemporal symmetry to run parallel belief-propagation trajectories with early termination under real-time constraints.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing demands decoders that are both accurate and fast enough to keep up with repeated syndrome extraction, a tension that current qLDPC decoders do not resolve.
method: The authors exploit spatial symmetries of BB codes and temporal regularity of syndrome extraction to define a layered, spatiotemporally covariant decoding structure; they compress BP dynamics into a low-dimensional representation to detect failing trajectories early, run multiple perturbed BP trajectories in parallel with reseeding, tune message-passing parameters offline via simulated annealing, and implement a pipelined two-arm memory-augmented BP core at register-transfer level.
result: Circuit-level simulations of a BB code give a logical error rate of ~1e-6 at physical error rate 1e-3, while the RTL implementation at 250 MHz achieves a 16 ns BP iteration interval per arm and 173.8 ns mean input-to-result latency.
conclusion: Physically motivated decoding structure plus algorithmic parallelism and dedicated hardware can bring accurate qLDPC decoding within real-time budgets, though the contribution is primarily engineering-oriented.

title: Coherence, Entanglement And Complementarity In Mixed Classical Light
authors: Asma Al-Qasimi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The classical analogues of quantum correlations have been the subject of considerable interest in the past few years; however, all of these investigations consider the classical analogue of pure quantum mechanical states only. In this work, we study mixed classical light states and derive relations between the polarization coherence of the field and the (classical) entanglement between its degrees of freedom. We show, for a specific model of mixed states, where the purity is determined by a single parameter, how the coherence shared between polarization and entanglement shrinks as the level of purity decreases. The sum of the square of polarization and entanglement remains constant, a behaviour consistent with previous results [Phys. Rev. Lett. 117, 153901 (2016)] of pure states, even though the constant for the mixed state case is now smaller in value.
tldr: The paper analyzes how polarization coherence and classical entanglement trade off in mixed classical light states as purity decreases.
motivation: Classical analogues of quantum correlations have mainly been studied for pure states, leaving mixed-state behavior and complementarity relations underexplored.
method: It considers a specific model of mixed classical light states parameterized by a single purity parameter and derives relations between polarization coherence and classical entanglement between degrees of freedom.
result: For the model, the sum of squared polarization coherence and squared classical entanglement remains constant but at a smaller value than in the pure-state case.
conclusion: The findings extend pure-state complementarity relations to mixed classical light and clarify how coherence is shared between polarization and classical entanglement as purity decreases.

They show that as the purity decreases, the coherence shared between polarization and entanglement shrinks, but the sum of the squares of polarization and entanglement remains constant. This constant is smaller than the value found for pure states in previous work (Phys. Rev. Lett. 117, 153901 (2016)). The analysis is based on classical coherence theory and the notion of classical entanglement, which arises from nonseparable correlations between degrees of freedom of a classical field. The paper provides a quantitative model for how mixedness affects the trade-off between polarization coherence and entanglement, offering a classical analogue to quantum mixed-state entanglement behavior.

title: Study Of Randomness In Quantum Random Number Generator Using Bayesian Neural Networks
authors: Shriram Pragash M, Aditi Das, Megha Shrivastava, Mohit Mittal, R. Srikanth, Venkat Abhignan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a Bayesian neural network (BNN) framework to quantify the intrinsic (aleatoric) uncertainty in a continuous-variable quantum random number generator (CV-QRNG). This provides a direct data-driven measure of the QRNG's randomness generation. The BNN is trained on raw homodyne voltage time-series data from a fiber-coupled vacuum-fluctuation QRNG (VFQRNG). For each voltage data segment, the network predicts a Gaussian distribution (mean and variance) for the next sample, and the ensemble-averaged predicted variance is used as a diagnostic of entropy-related behavior under assumptions of our quantum source model. Thus, the predicted variance serves as a BNN model-based monitor of the randomness-generation process. We validate that the BNN metric increases with the local-oscillator (LO) power, consistent with theoretical min-entropy (extractable randomness). We also show the metric is sensitive to practical imperfections, coarse-graining (simulating limited analog-to-digital converter (ADC) sampling) or reducing ADC bit depth causes a clear drop in predicted aleatoric uncertainty, consistent with the source min-entropic model. These results establish the BNN-based metric as a complementary, physically motivated diagnostic tool for QRNG characterization. Unlike conventional tests (e.g. autocorrelation) that miss hardware issues like low ADC resolution, our method provides a direct real-time monitor of the VFRNG performance. Therefore, this metric is useful for real-time monitoring of CV-QRNG conditions, including drifts and other imperfections.
tldr: The paper uses a Bayesian neural network to monitor randomness generation in a continuous-variable vacuum-fluctuation quantum random number generator via predicted aleatoric uncertainty.
motivation: Conventional statistical tests such as autocorrelation may miss practical hardware imperfections in QRNGs, motivating a data-driven diagnostic for real-time randomness monitoring.
method: A BNN is trained on raw homodyne voltage time-series from a fiber-coupled VFQRNG; for each segment it predicts a Gaussian distribution for the next sample, and ensemble-averaged predicted variance is used as an entropy-related diagnostic.
result: The BNN metric increases with local-oscillator power, consistent with theoretical min-entropy, and drops under coarse-graining or reduced ADC bit depth, consistent with source min-entropic behavior.
conclusion: The BNN-based metric is proposed as a complementary, physically motivated real-time diagnostic for CV-QRNG characterization, though it is not a replacement for rigorous randomness certification.

title: Certifying Quantum Generative Models Beyond The Fisher Trace
authors: Kathleen Hamilton Vicente Leyton-Ortega
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether a trained quantum generative model has learned its target is usually decided by a diagnostic validated on a labeled benchmark, and such a diagnostic can pass that validation by recovering how the benchmark was built. We analyze Fisher-trace and kernel-based certification of the real-amplitude quantum circuit Born machine in noiseless statevector simulation. For real-amplitude circuits built from half-angle rotations, the classical Fisher information equals the quantum Fisher information almost everywhere, so its trace equals the parameter count and carries no information about fit quality. The Fisher eigenvalue rank counts the live nodes of the amplitude tree: it coincides with the label on a sparse benchmark and is uninformative on a full-support one. The pooled Wasserstein and maximum-mean-discrepancy scores move with optimizer convergence and with the scoring convention. For two bitstring defect families on which both metrics have closed forms, we compute the tolerance-mismatch window in which the discrepancy rejects generators that the transport threshold admits; it opens only at certification-grade tolerances and closes as the qubit number grows. On the Hamming cost we prove a sharp tolerance ratio above which the discrepancy vote is redundant, and we obtain the exact worst-parity minimax value over all unit-diagonal positive-semidefinite kernels, which is exponentially small in the qubit number. In a numerical campaign at the tolerances a near-term experiment can resolve, the discrepancy vote changed no verdict at a thousand shots or more. The false-pass guarantee does not extend to device noise.
tldr: The paper analyzes certification diagnostics for real-amplitude quantum circuit Born machines, showing that Fisher-trace and kernel-based metrics can be uninformative or convention-dependent.
motivation: Quantum generative models need reliable certification, but common diagnostics may pass validation by exploiting benchmark construction rather than demonstrating true learning.
method: The authors study Fisher-trace, quantum/classical Fisher information, kernel MMD, and Wasserstein metrics in noiseless statevector simulations, deriving tolerance-mismatch windows and minimax kernel bounds.
result: Fisher trace equals parameter count almost everywhere for half-angle real-amplitude circuits and carries no fit-quality information; kernel discrepancy rarely changes verdicts at experimentally resolvable tolerances.
conclusion: Standard Fisher-trace and kernel-based certification can fail to certify quantum generative models meaningfully, and false-pass guarantees do not extend to device noise.

title: Hidden Momenta Due To Magneto-Electric Coupling In Non-Reciprocal Media
authors: William S. Mcgregor, Niclas Westerberg, Robert Bennett
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: From a canonical quantisation approach of macroscopic quantum electrodynamics, we derive the interaction Hamiltonian due to a dipole emitter interacting with a time-symmetry-broken topological insulator (TSB-TI), described by an axionic coupling Lagrangian. This provides an additional interaction term dependent on the magneto-electric coupling strength inherent to the TSB-TI which will modify measurements on related observables. The spontaneous decay rate is calculated in the Born-Markov approximation for a general electromagnetic Green's tensor, and then specifically for the case of a planar parallel-plate cavity.
tldr: The paper derives a modified dipole-emitter interaction Hamiltonian and spontaneous decay rate for emitters near a time-symmetry-broken topological insulator with magneto-electric coupling.
motivation: Macroscopic QED treatments of non-reciprocal media often neglect magneto-electric coupling; the authors aim to quantify how this coupling alters emitter observables.
method: They canonically quantize macroscopic QED with an axionic coupling Lagrangian and compute the spontaneous decay rate in the Born-Markov approximation for a general Green's tensor and a planar parallel-plate cavity.
result: An additional interaction term proportional to the magneto-electric coupling appears and modifies the spontaneous decay rate and related observables.
conclusion: Magneto-electric coupling in time-symmetry-broken topological insulators can produce observable corrections to spontaneous emission, which may matter for emitter-based quantum-optical platforms.

title: Efficient Simulation Of The Generalized Langevin Equation Using A Basis Of Dynamically Relevant Histories For Memory And Noise
authors: Evgeny Polyakov Dmitriy Kondaurov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19128v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Generalized Langevin Equation (GLE) is a cornerstone for modeling non-Markovian dynamics, but its numerical solution remains challenging due to the history-dependent convolution and the need to generate colored noise with a prescribed correlation function. We introduce a forward construction that addresses both challenges within a single framework. We represent an arbitrary trajectory as sum of relevant and irrelevant parts, where relevant part can be decomposed into a small number of characteristic history patterns that make the main contribution to future dynamics. It allows to reduce numerical cost to \(O(d^2)\) for [MATH] chosen patterns instead of full history. The same construction applies to colored noise generation, where the causal filter plays the role of the memory kernel. We demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the method for several representative kernels, including long-range kernels with power-law tails.
tldr: The paper introduces a numerical method to efficiently simulate the generalized Langevin equation by representing memory and colored noise through a small set of dynamically relevant history patterns.
motivation: Solving the generalized Langevin equation is computationally challenging because of the history-dependent convolution and the need to generate colored noise with a prescribed correlation function.
method: The authors decompose trajectories into relevant and irrelevant parts, approximate the relevant part using characteristic history patterns, and apply the same construction to colored noise generation via a causal filter.
result: The method reduces numerical cost to O(d^2) for d chosen patterns instead of requiring the full history, and is demonstrated on several kernels including long-range power-law tails.
conclusion: The proposed framework offers an efficient and unified approach for simulating non-Markovian dynamics and generating colored noise, though it is a classical numerical method rather than a quantum information or quantum thermodynamics result.

title: Metamorphic Testing Of Quantum Software Based On Stabilizer States
authors: Adri\'an Mar\'in Boyero, Fynn Otto, Albert Rico, Otfried G\"uhne, Malte Lochau
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A major challenge in quantum computing is to systematically check if a quantum program implements its desired functionality. For classical programs, testing is widely used; each test case comprises a pair of sample input and expected output to be compared with the actual output. To increase the number of test cases, however, one has to solve the test-oracle problem: for each additional test input one has to know the correct output. Metamorphic testing tackles this problem by utilizing metamorphic relations between input and output domains to automatically derive new test cases from existing ones. However, adapting metamorphic testing to the quantum realm is not straightforward, since quantum states cannot be directly inspected. We propose a framework of quantum metamorphic testing (QMT) in which the metamorphic relations incorporate the measurement procedures required to assess quantum outputs. We apply our QMT framework to testing the preparation of stabilizer states, which are central to protocols like measurement-based quantum computing or quantum error correction. We utilize structural properties of stabilizer states to systematically derive measurement circuits for new test cases from existing ones. We implement this framework in Qiskit, and demonstrate that it reduces by an order of magnitude the testing run time compared to testing with randomly generated input states. We further show effectiveness by revealing synthetic program faults injected by circuit mutations, as well as a real bug in the Qiskit compiler.
tldr: Proposes a quantum metamorphic testing framework that uses stabilizer-state structure to generate measurement circuits and detect faults in quantum programs.
motivation: Quantum software needs systematic testing, but quantum states cannot be directly inspected and the test-oracle problem limits the generation of new test cases.
method: Defines metamorphic relations that incorporate the measurement procedures needed to assess quantum outputs, applies the framework to stabilizer-state preparation, and implements it in Qiskit.
result: The framework reduces testing runtime by an order of magnitude compared with random input states and detects synthetic circuit-mutation faults plus a real bug in the Qiskit compiler.
conclusion: Quantum metamorphic testing is an effective approach for testing stabilizer-state quantum software and can reveal practical compiler faults.

title: A Quasipolynomial Quantum Algorithm For The Vector Dihedral Coset Problem With Smooth Modulus
authors: Aparna Gupte
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a quantum algorithm for the vector dihedral coset problem over [MATH], in which the goal is to recover [MATH] given independent samples of the form [MATH], for [MATH]. When the modulus [MATH] is [MATH]-smooth, the algorithm uses [MATH] samples and time. For [MATH] and [MATH], this gives a quasipolynomial time- and sample-complexity. This extends the previously known quasipolynomial-time result for power-of-two moduli (Bonnetain, Naya-Plasencia, ASIACRYPT 2018; Bai, Jangir, Kirshanova, Ngo, Youmans, CRYPTO 2025). The algorithm proceeds by reducing the modulus one prime factor [MATH] at a time. The key ingredient is a sieving procedure that clears the non-linear terms in the phase modulo [MATH] via an algorithm of Ivanyos, Santha (TCS 2017) that finds non-zero [MATH] such that [MATH] for degrees [MATH], given vectors [MATH] as input. The algorithm also applies to the extrapolated dihedral coset problem (EDCP) introduced by Brakerski, Kirshanova, Stehl\'e, Wen (PKC 2018), which is known to be equivalent to LWE in the polynomial sample regime. However, our result does not yield a new attack on LWE in any regime, precisely because the known reduction from LWE to EDCP provides only polynomially many clean samples, whereas our algorithm requires quasipolynomially many samples. The main algorithm was obtained in a GPT-5.6 Sol conversation prompted by the author; the author is responsible for all statements, proofs, and correctness. Concurrent work of Boucher, Fouque, Shen gives an algorithm with similar guarantees for prime-power moduli.
tldr: A quantum algorithm solving the vector dihedral coset problem over smooth moduli in quasipolynomial time and samples, by reducing the modulus one prime factor at a time.
motivation: The dihedral coset problem underlies several cryptographic constructions and was previously solvable in quasipolynomial time only for power-of-two moduli; extending this to smooth moduli broadens the class of tractable instances.
method: The algorithm reduces the modulus prime factor by prime factor, using a sieving procedure (based on an Ivanyos–Santha polynomial-systems algorithm) that clears non-linear phase terms modulo each prime, and also extends to the extrapolated DCP.
result: For smooth M with small prime factors the algorithm runs with quasipolynomial sample and time complexity; however, since the LWE-to-EDCP reduction supplies only polynomially many clean samples, no new attack on LWE follows.
conclusion: The work generalizes prior quasipolynomial-time DCP algorithms from power-of-two to smooth moduli, but does not improve cryptanalytic consequences for LWE.

title: Flexible Ground-state Search Algorithm On Hybrid Clifford-tensor Network Manifolds
authors: Hari Timsina, Antonio Francesco Mello, Meghadeepa Adhikary, Marcello Dalmonte, Mario Collura
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18848v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tensor network algorithms face challenges in highly entangled regimes, such as systems with periodic boundary conditions (PBC), long-range interactions, or higher dimensions, where the required bond dimension quickly renders computations infeasible. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that integrates the stabilizer formalism directly into the traditional density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) algorithm. While previous methods have used Clifford unitaries to minimize ground-state entanglement, fundamentally limited to distilling that away utilizing local two-qubit operations, our framework optimizes Clifford transformations to minimize the state's energy. We benchmark our method against standard DMRG at fixed bond dimensions for the Ising model on a ring (including long-range interactions) and on a torus. We observe systematic gains in models with local interactions - as drastic as a factor of 40 decrease in bond dimension in two dimensions. Our algorithm is readily implementable in standard DMRG codes and provides a practical way to substantially reduce algorithm costs, paving the way for large-scale simulation at volumes beyond what is presently achievable.
tldr: The paper introduces a hybrid Clifford-tensor network algorithm that integrates stabilizer transformations into DMRG to reduce bond dimension for ground-state searches in highly entangled regimes.
motivation: Tensor network methods such as DMRG become computationally infeasible for periodic boundary conditions, long-range interactions, and higher dimensions because required bond dimensions grow rapidly.
method: The authors optimize Clifford unitaries within a DMRG workflow to minimize ground-state energy rather than merely disentangle the state, and benchmark the approach against standard DMRG at fixed bond dimension.
result: For Ising models on a ring, with long-range interactions, and on a torus, the method shows systematic gains, including up to a factor of 40 reduction in bond dimension in two dimensions.
conclusion: The approach is readily implementable in standard DMRG codes and may enable larger-scale tensor network simulations beyond currently feasible volumes.

title: Double-Randomized Quantum Singular Value Transformations For Early Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers
authors: Joel Bierman, Pawan Poudel, Yuan Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) is an algorithmic framework which encompasses a wide range of problems, including Hamiltonian dynamics, ground state preparation, Gibbs state preparation, amplitude amplification, and matrix inversion. For many areas of scientific interest such as quantum chemistry and condensed matter, the circuit depth of the block-encoding subroutine in QSVT can be formidable, limiting the scope of problems to which QSVT can be applied on early fault-tolerant hardware. We split linear operators [MATH] into a core operator [MATH] and a tail operator [MATH], block-encoding the normalized sum of [MATH] and the average of [MATH] randomly sampled terms from [MATH]. We show that using randomized block-encodings of this form allows one to lower the circuit depth of QSVT while incurring a diamond norm error that scales as [MATH]), where [MATH] is a prefactor which depends on the QSVT polynomial [MATH] and [MATH] is the ratio of the [MATH] norms of the coefficient vectors of [MATH] and [MATH]. We then go on to show that if one samples QSVT circuits from a joint probability distribution of both random block-encodings and random polynomials (Double-Randomized QSVT), then the circuit depth savings of these two randomization techniques combine multiplicatively, with only additive error contributions. We numerically calculate error bounds for long-range Heisenberg and iron-sulfur complex Hamiltonians, showing that for a diamond norm error bound of [MATH], RBE-QSVT can reduce the number of Pauli terms needed for the block-encoding by an order of magnitude or more in several cases. This paves the way for demonstrations of QSVT on early fault-tolerant hardware.
