To address local smoothing bias that can distort confidence interval coverage, we further develop a debiased estimator that supports asymptotically valid pointwise inference without undersmoothing. Under additional uniform conditions, we construct simultaneous confidence bands using a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap. Simulation studies evaluate estimation accuracy, the validity of pointwise and uniform inference, and robustness to nuisance model misspecification. A semi-synthetic study calibrated to NHANES illustrates the proposed methods in a setting with a known dose-response function.
tldr: The paper develops multiply robust estimators for the average dose-response function when treatment duration is right-censored and outcomes are missing for censored units.
motivation: Standard dose-response estimation assumes fully observed treatment levels; censored treatment durations and missing outcomes break this, requiring new identification and estimation strategies.
method: Using duration lower bounds from censored records, the authors build augmented local estimating equations to obtain a multiply robust estimator, plus a debiased version for valid pointwise inference and Gaussian multiplier bootstrap confidence bands under cross-fitting.
result: The estimator is consistent if any two of the outcome regression, treatment density, and censoring survival functions are correctly specified, with established convergence rates and asymptotic distribution; simulations and an NHANES-calibrated semi-synthetic study confirm accuracy and coverage.
conclusion: The framework provides robust, asymptotically valid pointwise and uniform inference for dose-response curves under right-censored treatment, extending causal inference methodology rather than addressing quantum information questions.

title: Spectral Gaps And Low-Energy Modes In Anisotropic High-Contrast PDEs
authors: Yajun Wang, Eric T. Chung, Lijian Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the low-energy spectrum of high-contrast partial differential equations with strongly anisotropic inclusions. The inclusion stiffness and mass are scaled by a contrast parameter \(\eta\), while a small material eigenvalue \(\epsilon\) controls anisotropy. Stable extensions of local kernel fields give eigenvalue upper bounds proportional to the inverse contrast, uniformly in anisotropy. Additional low-energy modes arise from fields whose nonzero differential images lie in weak material directions. Each fixed family of compatible weak fields yields additional eigenvalue upper bounds of order [MATH], provided a stable extension exists. Under discrete stability assumptions, we obtain corresponding finite element bounds for the weak modes represented by the mesh. For separable scalar diffusion, we prove norm-resolvent convergence to independent background Dirichlet and inclusion Neumann operators as contrast tends to infinity with anisotropy fixed. Numerical experiments for four PDE models illustrate weak modes and mesh-dependent spectral transitions, and scalar diffusion experiments also test spectral decoupling and eigenvalue counting.
tldr: The paper analyzes low-energy spectra of anisotropic high-contrast PDEs, deriving eigenvalue bounds and finite-element approximations for weak low-energy modes.
motivation: High-contrast PDEs with anisotropic inclusions exhibit complicated low-energy spectra that are important for multiscale modeling and numerical simulation.
method: The authors use stable extensions of local kernel fields, weak-field constructions, finite-element stability assumptions, and norm-resolvent convergence analysis in the separable scalar diffusion case.
result: They obtain eigenvalue upper bounds proportional to inverse contrast, additional bounds from compatible weak fields, finite-element bounds for mesh-represented weak modes, and prove spectral decoupling in the separable scalar diffusion limit.
conclusion: The work clarifies how anisotropy and contrast produce low-energy modes and mesh-dependent spectral transitions in high-contrast PDE models.

title: Many Faces Of Integer Semidefinite Programming
authors: Renata Sotirov Mirjam D\"{u}r
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We first establish several properties of integer positive semidefinite matrices, extending known results for binary and ternary positive semidefinite matrices. We then show how to reformulate an integer quadratic program (IQP) as an equivalent integer semidefinite program (ISDP). We distinguish three cases, namely IQPs with two, three, or more than three distinct integer values, and provide several ISDPs for each case. Each reformulation yields either a binary ISDP, a ternary ISDP, or a rescaled version of one of these. The results show that ternary SDP formulations for problems with three distinct integer values provide SDP relaxations with fewer constraints and, in the case of equally spaced integers, also smaller matrix variables than binary-based SDP relaxations. For quadratic problems whose variables can take more than three distinct integer values, one can choose among three formulations based on the size of their matrix variables, the number of constraints, and the strength of the resulting SDP relaxations. We also show how to reformulate a mixed-integer QP as a mixed-integer SDP.
tldr: The paper studies integer positive semidefinite matrices and reformulates integer quadratic programs as integer semidefinite programs using binary, ternary, or rescaled formulations.
motivation: Integer semidefinite programming is less developed than binary semidefinite programming, and the authors aim to extend structural results and solution reformulations for integer quadratic optimization.
method: The authors establish properties of integer positive semidefinite matrices and derive equivalent integer semidefinite programming formulations for IQPs with two, three, or more than three distinct integer values, including mixed-integer extensions.
result: They show that ternary SDP formulations can have fewer constraints and, for equally spaced integers, smaller matrix variables than binary-based SDP relaxations; for more than three values, multiple formulations offer tradeoffs in matrix size, constraint count, and relaxation strength.
conclusion: The work provides a systematic framework for reformulating integer and mixed-integer quadratic programs as integer semidefinite programs, with practical guidance on choosing formulations.

title: Multidimensional Mixed Bohr Radii For Banach Space Valued Holomorphic Functions
authors: Raju Biswas Vasudevarao Allu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we introduce and study a generalized notion of multidimensional mixed Bohr radii for holomorphic functions defined on the unit ball of the finite-dimensional Minkowski sequence space with values in complex Banach spaces. We first prove that the multidimensional mixed Bohr radius is positive for every non-null bounded linear operator whose norm is sufficiently small relative to the scaling parameter. We then determine the exact asymptotic behavior of the multidimensional mixed Bohr radius for infinite-dimensional Banach spaces of finite cotype and we obtain analogous bounds for spaces without finite cotype. Finally, for concave Banach lattices and summing operators, we prove lower bounds that involve a logarithmic factor. These results connect classical scalar Bohr phenomena with operator-valued and Banach space valued settings, and highlight how the geometry of the spaces and the mapping properties of the operator influence coefficient estimates and their dependence on dimension. Several examples illustrate the consistency of our results with the classical Bohr radius and the sharp Defant--Frerick asymptotics.
tldr: The paper introduces and analyzes multidimensional mixed Bohr radii for Banach-space-valued holomorphic functions on the unit ball of finite-dimensional Minkowski sequence spaces.
motivation: Classical Bohr phenomena (power series coefficient bounds) are well studied for scalar functions, and the authors aim to extend them to operator-valued and Banach-space-valued settings in multiple dimensions.
method: They prove positivity of the mixed Bohr radius for bounded linear operators of small norm, derive exact asymptotics for finite-cotype Banach spaces, bound cotype-free cases, and establish logarithmic lower bounds for concave Banach lattices and summing operators.
result: The multidimensional mixed Bohr radius is shown to be positive under a small-norm condition, with sharp Defant–Frerick-type asymptotics in finite cotype and logarithmic corrections in the concave lattice and summing-operator settings.
conclusion: The work links scalar Bohr phenomena to operator- and Banach-space-valued holomorphic function theory, showing how space geometry and operator mapping properties govern coefficient estimates and dimensional dependence.

title: Operating-Point Failure Of Frozen Guardrail Probes Under Backbone Updates
authors: Sang-Chul Kim Yusuf Khalid Shire
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We freeze a guardrail probe and threshold, then measure its operating point across 18 cells covering 16 public language-model updates. At a 1% target, the threshold fails closed in 8 of 9 cells in the first phase and either fails closed or open in 3 of 9 cells in a registered second phase (descriptive). The two phases also differ in update type and input format. The largest increase is from 1.01% to 15.12%, while the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve changes by no more than 0.0058 in any of these cells. A benchmark's staleness criteria classify none of them as stale. A rule based on these criteria flags 0.019 of layer cells where the rate doubles or halves. A label-free rate estimate flags 0.918, clearing 0.898 of the remaining cells. A two-moment model matches the change within a factor of 1.5 in 0.905 of 63 registered cells and in 0.773 of the 22 cells that moved. Resetting the threshold using stored benign prompts restores the false-positive rate without requiring new labels. However, poisoning 1% of these prompts leaves at most 0.017 of harmful prompts flagged. An attacker controlling the update cut detection of one of three targeted categories in three of five seeds. Both checks missed this attack, while a post hoc labelled check detected it.
tldr: The paper shows that frozen guardrail probes for language models silently mis-calibrate their operating point when backbone models are updated, and that benchmark staleness criteria fail to detect this drift.
motivation: Deployed safety classifiers (guardrail probes) are often frozen while the underlying language models they monitor are repeatedly updated, so the authors ask whether threshold-based operating points remain valid across model updates.
method: They fix a probe and threshold, measure false-positive and detection rates across 18 cells spanning 16 public model updates in two phases, compare against staleness criteria, and propose label-free rate estimation plus a two-moment model for recalibration using stored benign prompts.
result: At a 1% target the threshold fails closed in 8 of 9 cells in phase one and misbehaves in 3 of 9 cells in phase two, with rates rising from 1.01% to 15.12% while AUROC changes by at most 0.0058; existing staleness criteria flag none of these cells, and prompt poisoning or attacker-controlled updates defeat the label-free recalibration while a post hoc labelled check catches the attack.
conclusion: Operating-point drift under backbone updates is a real and currently undetected failure mode for frozen guardrail probes, and label-free recalibration helps but is itself vulnerable to poisoning, motivating post hoc labelled audits.

title: Towards Understanding The Complexity Of Caqe: A Proof-Theoretic Analysis Of Its Core Procedure
authors: Olaf Beyersdorff Benjamin B\"ohm
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CAQE (Clausal Abstraction for Quantifier Elimination) is currently the most successful algorithmic paradigm for solving Quantified Boolean Formulas (QBF) in practice, clearly dominating recent QBF competitions. While apparently being a very strong solver, not much is known about CAQE in theory. We propose a framework for formalising runs of the basic CAQE algorithm (where failed assumptions are not considered) as proofs in a proof system CAQE[MATH], which we use to analyse the algorithm proof-theoretically and which provides methods for future work to separate it from optimised versions of CAQE that are used in practice. We show that one can perform strategy extraction on the CAQE[MATH] proof system in such a way that strategy size serves as a lower bound for basic CAQE runs. Furthermore, we introduce a measure, which we call CAQE width, which not only acts as a lower bound on CAQE[MATH] proofs, but -- with the number of [MATH] alternations as exponent -- as an upper bound as well. Using this analysis, we prove that Q-resolution with an NP oracle simulates CAQE[MATH] on QCNFs of bounded quantifier alternation. The same holds for QCDCL (Quantified Conflict-Driven Clause Learning, formalised as a proof system) on [MATH] QCNFs when purely propositional CDCL steps are not counted, after a simple preprocessing step. In this setting, both systems are indeed strictly stronger than CAQE[MATH], where the separation of QCDCL from CAQE[MATH] uses cube learning.
tldr: The paper formalises runs of the basic CAQE QBF-solving algorithm as proofs in a new proof system, using proof-theoretic tools to bound strategy size and CAQE width and to compare CAQE against Q-resolution-with-oracle and QCDCL.
motivation: CAQE dominates practical QBF solving but has almost no theoretical underpinning, so the authors aim to give a formal, proof-theoretic account of why and when the algorithm works.
method: They introduce the CAQE proof system capturing runs of basic CAQE, prove strategy extraction giving lower bounds from strategy size, define a 'CAQE width' measure that lower- and upper-bounds proof size, and use these to establish simulation results by Q-resolution with an NP oracle and by QCDCL (modulo propositional CDCL steps) on bounded-alternation QCNFs.
result: They show Q-resolution with an NP oracle simulates CAQE on bounded-alternation QCNFs, that the same holds for QCDCL after preprocessing, and that both systems are strictly stronger, with the QCDCL separation exploiting cube learning.
conclusion: The framework provides the first rigorous proof-theoretic analysis of CAQE and a basis for separating the basic algorithm from its optimised practical variants.

title: A Recursive Construction Of Perfect And Odd Perfect Sequences Of Unbounded Length Over The Unit Quaternions
authors: Sam Blake
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a recursive construction, with closed-form index functions, of perfect and odd perfect periodic autocorrelation sequences over the eight simple unit quaternions [MATH] in every length [MATH]. The sequences are built, as in the recursive perfect array construction of Blake, from : a short sequence continued with period [MATH] up to a right factor [MATH]. Over roots of unity the twists cannot be regenerated by a one-dimensional recursion, consistently with Mow's conjecture; over [MATH] we show that no single sequence of length [MATH] carries a twist [MATH] or [MATH] either, but that of sequences whose [MATH]- and [MATH]-twisted autocorrelations are complementary do. These [MATH]-pairs behave exactly like Golay pairs: they double under interleaving with a right factor [MATH] in place of a sign, every Golay pair of length [MATH] gives an [MATH]-pair of length [MATH], and they exist in length [MATH] where no Golay pair exists. An [MATH]-pair of length [MATH] interleaves to an odd perfect sequence of length [MATH], and a perfect and an odd perfect sequence of length [MATH] interleave to a perfect sequence of length [MATH] with the array orthogonality property for the divisor [MATH]. The [MATH]-pairs of length [MATH] are [MATH], where [MATH] counts the changes in the bit string formed by [MATH] and the binary digits of [MATH], and the odd perfect sequence of length [MATH] is [MATH]. The construction also gives odd perfect sequences over [MATH] in every length [MATH] and perfect sequences in every length [MATH].
tldr: The paper gives a recursive, closed-form construction of perfect and odd perfect periodic autocorrelation sequences over the eight unit quaternions, for every length, along with Golay-like quaternion-pair structures.
motivation: Perfect and odd perfect autocorrelation sequences are useful for signal design, radar, and communications, but known constructions over roots of unity are limited by constraints such as Mow's conjecture; the authors seek a richer alphabet where recursive one-dimensional construction is possible.
method: Sequences are built recursively by extending a short sequence with a period up to a right factor, using twists by the imaginary units i, j, k; the authors analyze when twisted autocorrelations are complementary and show these 'q-pairs' behave like Golay pairs under interleaving.
result: Quaternion pairs double under interleaving with a right factor, every Golay pair yields a quaternion pair, quaternion pairs exist in lengths where no Golay pair exists, and interleaving yields odd perfect and perfect sequences with the array orthogonality property; explicit closed forms are given for the pairs and sequences.
conclusion: The construction provides perfect and odd perfect sequences over the unit quaternions in every length, extending classical sequence design beyond roots of unity and producing new combinatorial objects with Golay-like properties.

title: Attacker Diversity Reduction In Adaptive Llm Red Teaming
authors: Chris Tava
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning can make automated red-teaming more successful while narrowing the attacks it produces. Co-training an attacker and a defender with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been reported to reduce attacker diversity. This experiment reproduces attack diversity reduction using three runs with a Qwen2.5-14B attacker and a Phi-4-mini defender trained by direct preference optimization (DPO). The attacker receives a success-only reward and uses a length-unbiased loss, bounded updates, warm-up and ratio clipping. The attacker is evaluated on 26 AdvBench behaviors. Training ended after 12 rounds, following a decision based on development checkpoints, so the reported intervals are nominal. Attack Diversity Retention (ADR) compares the within-behavior of the trained attacker spread with the untrained attacker. In order for an attack diversity to be consider as having been reduced, a criterion requires the ADR to be below a 0.75 target with a 95% confidence interval together with continued attacker effectiveness. Therefore, if an attacker narrows its attack vector by 25% consistently its considered less diverse. After 24 attacker and 12 defender LORA-based updates, ADR for the three runs were 0.63, 0.61 and 0.63, respectively. Each run met the criterion at round 12; the earlier checks at rounds 4 and 8 fell short. Despite attacks being less diverse, attack success continued to improve as the attacker was updated after each training run.
tldr: A reproduction study showing that RL-based co-training of an LLM attacker and defender reduces the diversity of generated adversarial attacks while attack success continues to rise.
motivation: Automated red-teaming using reinforcement learning against LLMs can be highly effective, but there are reports that co-training attacker and defender models collapses the attacker's attack repertoire, limiting coverage of harmful behaviors.
method: Three runs with a Qwen2.5-14B attacker and a Phi-4-mini defender trained by DPO; the attacker uses GRPO-style group-relative updates with a success-only reward, length-unbiased loss, bounded updates, warm-up and ratio clipping, evaluated on 26 AdvBench behaviors over 12 rounds via an Attack Diversity Retention (ADR) metric.
result: ADR values of 0.63, 0.61 and 0.63 across the three runs at round 12, all below the 0.75 reduction criterion, while attack success rate continued to improve with further attacker updates. Intervals are only nominal since stopping was decided by development checkpoints.
conclusion: Co-training with GRPO-style attacker updates systematically narrows attack diversity even as effectiveness grows, suggesting a trade-off that red-teaming pipelines should monitor explicitly.

title: Local Order Matters: A Lightweight CPU-Trainable Cnn For Website Fingerprinting On Defended Tor Traffic
authors: Puyang Xu, Zhizhao Wen, Yifan Jiang, Chao Wang, Yusi Gong
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Website fingerprinting (WF) attacks let a passive adversary infer which site a Tor user visits from the encrypted cell sequence. On undefended traffic, hand-crafted-feature attacks are already near-ceiling, so deep learning offers only a marginal advantage there. We show that the decisive regime is defended traffic: against the FRONT padding defense, which injects dummy cells that corrupt the volume and count features feature attacks rely on, a compact 95,103-parameter 1-D convolutional network trained on the raw cell-direction sequence, on CPU only, stays robust while three implemented direction-only feature baselines degrade. On the closed-world WFlib FRONT set (95 sites), our model reaches 54.2% top-1 accuracy versus 38.5% for the strongest implemented feature baseline (k-FP-style RF), a gain of 15.7 percentage points (3 seeds; seed-0 paired-bootstrap 95% CI [+14.5, +17.0] pp on per-trace correctness, excluding zero). On undefended traffic the CNN reaches 94.1% versus 92.3% for k-FP-style RF. A controlled order-ablation permutes only nonzero traffic cells within each trace, preserving direction counts, retained length, and trailing zero-padding positions while destroying traffic order. This collapses the CNN below every feature baseline (from 54.2% to 7.6%, a 46.6 pp drop), showing that the model depends strongly on order-derived information under FRONT.
tldr: A compact 1-D CNN trained on raw Tor cell-direction sequences outperforms hand-crafted feature baselines against the FRONT padding defense, with an order-ablation showing the gain comes from traffic-order information.
motivation: Website fingerprinting against defended Tor traffic is where feature-based attacks break down, since padding defenses corrupt volume and count statistics; the authors ask whether a small sequence model can exploit ordering instead.
method: A 95,103-parameter 1-D convolutional network is trained CPU-only on raw cell-direction sequences and benchmarked against three direction-only feature baselines (including a k-FP-style random forest) on the WFlib FRONT closed-world set, plus a controlled permutation ablation that destroys order while preserving counts and padding.
result: Against FRONT the CNN reaches 54.2% top-1 versus 38.5% for the best feature baseline (+15.7 pp, 3 seeds, bootstrap CI [+14.5, +17.0] pp); on undefended traffic 94.1% versus 92.3%; permuting nonzero cells collapses accuracy to 7.6%.
conclusion: Sequence order is the decisive signal under padding defenses, and a lightweight CPU-trainable CNN suffices to exploit it, highlighting a privacy weakness in FRONT-style defenses.

title: Cyber-Secure Wearable, Ultra-Low-Power Networked Sensors For Soldier Health Monitoring: Insights From The Capsarii Project
authors: Luciano Bozzi, Christian Celidonio, Umberto Nuzzi, Massimo Biagini, Stefano Cherubin, Asbj{\o}rn Djupdal, Tor Andre Haugdahl, Andrea Aliverti, Alessandra Angelucci, Giovanni Agosta, Gerardo Pelosi, Paolo Belluco, Samuele Polistina, Gaia Strada, Luigi Sossi Ortega, Alexandra-Ioana Albu, Riccardo Volpi, Luigi Malag\`o, Michael Schneider, Xabier Eguiluz, Haritz Saiz, Mar\'ia Viqueria
abstract: ArXiv:2611.20187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The CAPSARII project advances a cyber-secure, ultra-low-power wearable platform and Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) framework to support real-time monitoring of military personnel and data-driven decision support. The architecture integrates smart-textile sensing, a body/squad area mesh, edge-deployed AI on secure RISC-V microcontrollers, and cloud/federated analytics for cross-mission learning and comparative studies. Two representative use cases--pilot fatigue and warfighters operating in harsh environments--guide requirements, validation, and interface design (including HUD and haptic feedback). As an initial step toward embedded models, we benchmark stress classification on a public wearable dataset: tree-ensemble baselines achieve state-of-the-art performance for accuracy and F1 (e.g., XGBoost: [MATH], [MATH]), while a feature-based Transformer attains the highest AUC ([MATH]), informing feature-engineering and compression choices for edge deployment. Building on these results, CAPSARII employs HW/SW co-design, model compression (pruning, quantization, distillation), and precision tuning to meet stringent energy and memory budgets; it further investigates Processing-in-Memory accelerators for future efficiency gains. A structured gap analysis highlights the remaining challenges: establishing validation standards for physiological signal quality and textile durability; achieving low-latency, scalable BAN/SAN communications under mobility and interference; and deploying hybrid lightweight/post-quantum cryptography with robust device identity and side-channel resilience on constrained endpoints. By consolidating these elements into a coherent, secure IoBT stack, CAPSARII delineates a practical roadmap from laboratory baselines to mission-ready soldier monitoring in both training and operational scenarios.
tldr: The CAPSARII project presents a cyber-secure, ultra-low-power wearable sensor and Internet of Battlefield Things framework for real-time soldier health monitoring and decision support.
motivation: Military personnel require continuous physiological monitoring in harsh environments, but existing wearable platforms must satisfy strict energy, security, and communication constraints.
method: The paper describes an architecture combining smart-textile sensing, body/squad area mesh networking, edge AI on secure RISC-V microcontrollers, and cloud/federated analytics, along with benchmarking of stress classification on a public wearable dataset.
result: Tree-ensemble baselines achieve state-of-the-art accuracy and F1, while a feature-based Transformer attains the highest AUC, informing feature engineering and compression choices for edge deployment.
conclusion: CAPSARII provides a roadmap toward mission-ready soldier monitoring and identifies remaining challenges in validation standards, low-latency scalable BAN/SAN communications, and hybrid lightweight/post-quantum cryptography on constrained endpoints.

title: Ai Climate Trajectories Shaped By Growth, Power Choices And Decarbonization
authors: Xiaoyu Xie, John Bistline, Ming Xu, Sangwon Suh
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19080v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a major source of electricity demand, yet its operational greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions remain difficult to resolve geographically. We develop a facility-level global inventory of AI-oriented data centers and extend it to 2030 using documented expansion plans and grid-policy scenarios. Under Current Policies, emissions increase from 20.4 MtCO[MATH]e in 2024 to 68.7 MtCO[MATH]e in 2030, with parameter-side Monte Carlo 5th--95th percentile ranges of 19.3--21.0 and 60.8--73.9 MtCO[MATH]e, respectively. Only six geographies, representing less than 3% of projected capacity, avoid rising emissions. Grid decarbonization consistent with net zero by 2050 lowers projected 2030 emissions to 48.3 MtCO[MATH]e, but fossil-based behind-the-meter generation erodes this benefit. Under that scenario, the U.S. behind-the-meter emissions penalty exceeds the combined AI-data-center emissions outside the United States. These findings support coordinated capacity planning, faster access to low-carbon electricity and limits on routine fossil-based behind-the-meter supply.
tldr: The paper inventories global AI data-center emissions and projects 2030 greenhouse-gas trajectories under growth, power-source, and grid-decarbonization scenarios.
motivation: AI's rapid electricity demand growth makes its operational greenhouse-gas emissions geographically difficult to resolve, motivating a facility-level global inventory and scenario analysis.
method: The authors build a facility-level inventory of AI-oriented data centers, extend it to 2030 using documented expansion plans and grid-policy scenarios, and perform Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis.
result: Under Current Policies, emissions rise from 20.4 MtCO2e in 2024 to 68.7 MtCO2e in 2030, while net-zero-consistent grid decarbonization lowers 2030 emissions to 48.3 MtCO2e but is eroded by fossil-based behind-the-meter generation.
conclusion: The findings support coordinated capacity planning, faster access to low-carbon electricity, and limits on routine fossil-based behind-the-meter supply for AI data centers.

title: Repairing Actuator Schedules Under Graph Constraints
authors: Piotr Kraso{\'n} Dawid E. K\k{e}dzierski
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19291v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a discrete-time linear system in which each actuator is assigned to one time slot. A graph [MATH] records which pairs of actuators cannot share a slot. We seek to remove conflicts by exchanging actuators between slots, while preserving all tail reachability spaces. These spaces describe the terminal corrections available from each time slot onward. We give a sufficient condition based on the number of exchanges that preserve the required bases. The condition guarantees repair from every compatible starting schedule. Two bounds for checking it use failed basis tests and dependent column selections. Each accepted exchange reduces the conflict count, so the procedure uses at most as many exchanges as there are initial conflicts. An explicit family with unequal rank increments admits repair when [MATH], where [MATH] is the largest number of forbidden partners of any actuator. We also give a family of two-slot examples with only one forbidden partner per actuator and two initial conflicts. The basis constraints force every strict improvement to move arbitrarily many actuators, although one exchange suffices without those constraints. A second example has a connected conflict graph and one initial conflict.
tldr: The paper studies repair of actuator schedules under graph constraints while preserving tail reachability spaces in discrete-time linear systems.
motivation: Actuator scheduling conflicts arise when certain actuators cannot share time slots, and repairs should preserve the terminal correction capabilities of the system.
method: The authors formulate schedule repair as exchanging actuators between slots under graph constraints and derive a sufficient condition based on the number of basis-preserving exchanges.
result: They provide bounds for checking the condition using failed basis tests and dependent column selections, show the procedure terminates within the number of initial conflicts, and construct examples illustrating rank and conflict-graph effects.
conclusion: The work gives graph-constrained schedule-repair guarantees for linear systems, but it is unrelated to quantum information, quantum thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Structural Latent Dimension: Deterministic Geometry And Local Fisher Structure
authors: Matteo Farn\`e
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the of a second-order object: the minimum latent dimension that remains necessary relative to a declared class of competing dependence. Building on minimum-rank factor analysis and low-rank-plus-sparse decomposition, we use distances to lower-dimensional classes to describe inference near structural ambiguity. General distance and tangent-cone facts yield confidence statements and local margins. For rank-zero competitors with bounded residual degree, we derive exact maximum-weight [MATH]-matching formulas, support-slack tangent cones and sparse-spike angles; a shared residual support across a field can produce separation absent pointwise. We give positive-semidefinite brackets, a dimension-free Gaussian likelihood expansion, an exact quotient by the tangent of a low-rank background, and a detection floor from the margin. Equal-angle configurations with different branch multiplicities motivate static and spectral detection conjectures. Joint low-rank/residual profiling and the sharp composite information boundaries remain open.
tldr: The paper studies a structural latent-dimension problem in statistical factor models using low-rank-plus-sparse geometry and local Fisher information.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize the minimum latent dimension needed relative to competing dependence classes and to quantify inference near structural ambiguity.
method: They use minimum-rank factor analysis, low-rank-plus-sparse decomposition, distances to lower-dimensional classes, tangent-cone geometry, and Gaussian likelihood expansions.
result: They derive exact maximum-weight matching formulas for rank-zero competitors, support-slack tangent cones, sparse-spike angles, positive-semidefinite brackets, and a detection floor from local margins.
conclusion: The work provides geometric and Fisher-information tools for latent-dimension inference, while joint low-rank/residual profiling and sharp composite information boundaries remain open.

title: ElevatorII: High-Performance Fully-Static Cross-ISA Binary Translation
authors: Hongyu Chen, James Mcgowan, Michael Franz
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19577v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The established method for running software compiled for one instruction-set architecture (ISA) on a different ISA is by emulation in conjunction with just-in-time (JIT) compilation. This requires run-time support on the target that needs to be trusted and whose compilation decisions are hard to predict or reconstruct. We present ElevatorII, a fully static, ahead-of-time cross-ISA binary-to-binary compiler from x86 to AArch64 that challenges the established consensus. Our approach eliminates the need for run-time support on the target, removes the hard to reproduce effects of dynamic compilation, and provides the capability to exhaustively test the actual binary that is eventually executed. Our approach combines superset disassembly with observation-guided path selection. Superset disassembly overcomes the code vs. data differentiation problem by creating a separate control flow path for every possible interpretation of every byte in the input binary. It guarantees that there is pre-translated code for every possible jump destination in the original text segment, even for computed jumps that are not statically decidable. Static and observation-guided path selection then creates additional optimized "confirmed code paths" that overlay the regular grid. On the 11 SPEC CPU 2026 Integer benchmarks that do not use C++ exceptions, ElevatorII runs at 2.5x native AArch64 time, on par with Box64, the fastest dynamic translator, and 5x faster than QEMU. It also translates binaries obfuscated with virtualization and branch functions, which no static disassembler can follow. Our approach trades execution performance for space: our output code is 51x the size of code compiled from source. We alleviate this by separating cold code to a .text.unlikely ELF section: only 2-3% hot code winds up in the main ELF section, while the rest will likely never be loaded into memory.
tldr: ElevatorII is a fully static x86-to-AArch64 binary translator that uses superset disassembly and observation-guided path selection to eliminate runtime JIT support.
motivation: Running software compiled for one ISA on another typically requires emulation plus JIT compilation, which introduces trusted runtime support and hard-to-reproduce dynamic compilation effects.
method: The authors combine superset disassembly, which creates pre-translated code paths for all possible byte interpretations, with observation-guided selection of optimized confirmed code paths.
result: On 11 SPEC CPU 2026 Integer benchmarks, ElevatorII runs at 2.5x native AArch64 time, comparable to Box64 and 5x faster than QEMU, while producing code 51x larger than source-compiled code.
conclusion: The work challenges the consensus that cross-ISA translation requires dynamic compilation and shows that fully static binary translation can be competitive while enabling exhaustive testing of the final binary.

title: An Analytic Two-Dimensional Benchmark For Integrated Autocorrelation Times In Branching Monte Carlo Part I: Transport Spectra And Branching Theory
authors: Jilang Miao, Guillaume L. Giudicelli, William Reed Kendrick
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting correlations between source generations can support uncertainty estimation and variance reduction in Monte Carlo transport. We derive a two-dimensional benchmark for planar isotropic exponential flights in a reflecting square. An image construction gives the exact collision and absorption spectra. Critical branching preserves the mean transport operator but changes mode covariances through the offspring second moment. These covariances give tally autocorrelations and integrated autocorrelation times, with a large-population, finite-window approximation for normalized source tallies. Direct Monte Carlo measurements test the predictions for absorption/rebirth and two-offspring fission. The benchmark provides a reference for assessing reduced correlation models, for correcting reported tally uncertainties, and for checking the tallies of a production code for correlation bias.
tldr: The paper derives an analytic two-dimensional benchmark for integrated autocorrelation times in branching Monte Carlo particle transport in a reflecting square.
motivation: Correlations between source generations affect uncertainty estimation and variance reduction in Monte Carlo transport, so a tractable reference benchmark is needed to validate reduced correlation models and tally uncertainties.
method: The authors solve planar isotropic exponential flights in a reflecting square via an image construction to obtain exact collision and absorption spectra, then incorporate critical branching (absorption/rebirth and two-offspring fission) to obtain mode covariances and a large-population finite-window approximation for normalized source tallies.
result: Analytic predictions for spectra, tally autocorrelations, and integrated autocorrelation times are validated against direct Monte Carlo measurements, providing a reference benchmark for correlation bias checks.
conclusion: The benchmark supports assessing reduced correlation models, correcting reported tally uncertainties, and checking production-code tallies for correlation bias.

title: Q-completely Monotonic And q-Bernstein Functions
authors: Valmir Krasniqi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For [MATH], we study (q)-completely monotone and q-Bernstein functions defined by the Jackson derivative. We establish the positive linear closure of the latter class and prove an integral characterization of q-Bernstein functions continuous at zero on a geometric lattice. The representing measures satisfy the natural L\'evy integrability condition, and the corresponding integral kernels are positive semidefinite. We prove that classical completely monotone and Bernstein functions belong to the respective q-classes and examine composition with absolutely monotone functions. Explicit examples show the limits of product closure, composition, and definiteness with respect to ordinary addition.
tldr: The paper develops q-analogues of completely monotone and Bernstein functions defined via the Jackson derivative, proving closure and integral representation results on a geometric lattice.
motivation: Classical completely monotone and Bernstein functions are central to probability, potential theory, and analysis; the authors aim to extend this framework to a q-deformed (Jackson-derivative) setting.
method: Using the Jackson derivative, they establish positive linear closure of q-Bernstein functions, prove an integral characterization for functions continuous at zero on a geometric lattice, verify Lévy-type integrability of representing measures and positive semidefiniteness of kernels, and test composition with absolutely monotone functions.
result: Classical completely monotone and Bernstein functions are shown to belong to the respective q-classes, while explicit examples reveal failures of product closure, composition, and definiteness under ordinary addition.
conclusion: The q-classes mirror but do not fully preserve classical structural properties, delineating the limits of the q-generalization.

title: Generalized Particle Systems: A Locality-factorized Metamodel For Self-propelled Particles And Agent-based Models
authors: Igor Strozzi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a single formal object, the generalized particle system (GPS), under which self-propelled particle systems (SPPS) and agent-based models (ABMs) are instances of one construction. A GPS is a typed finite population, a per-particle state space with arbitrary internal structure, a global environment, a neighbourhood map that may depend on the configuration, and type-indexed local rules; these assemble into a generator whose iteration is a monoid action, i.e. an autonomous dynamical system. Update schedules and stochastic rules are added at the same generality, so sequential and noisy models (the original Primordial Particle System, Vicsek) are covered, not approximated. The construction isolates the one ingredient separating the two communities: in the classical ABM reading the dependency graph is fixed; in an SPPS it is a function of the state. Under an exchangeability axiom (rules see neighbours only through the multiset of their types and states) the generator is equivariant for type-preserving permutations and descends to a dynamical system on counting measures, the setting of kinetic limits of swarming models. We read the tuple as a metamodel: its structural components coordinatize a space of models inside which numerical parameters live. Six pre-registered experiments on one engine implementing the generator test the claims: freezing the neighbourhood map destroys alignment ([MATH]) while yielding a different, non-aligned aggregation; the realized neighbourhood graph rewires up to 64% of its edges per step, its rewiring rate anti-correlated with order ([MATH]); a topological instead of metric neighbourhood reshapes a flocking phase diagram; the same rule with cohesion and separation off shows a Vicsek-type transition whose susceptibility peak grows with system size. One prediction failed and one subsumption claim is unconfirmed; both are reported.
tldr: The paper introduces a generalized particle system (GPS) metamodel that unifies self-propelled particle systems and agent-based models as instances of a single locality-factorized construction.
motivation: The self-propelled particle and agent-based modeling communities use formally similar but separately developed frameworks, and the authors aim to provide one formal object that subsumes both and clarifies where they diverge.
method: A GPS is defined as a typed finite population with per-particle state spaces, a global environment, a state-dependent neighbourhood map, and type-indexed local rules forming a monoid action; update schedules and stochasticity are added, with an exchangeability axiom enabling descent to dynamics on counting measures. Six pre-registered experiments on a single engine test structural claims.
result: Freezing the neighbourhood map destroys alignment while producing non-aligned aggregation; realized neighbourhood graphs rewire up to 64% of edges per step with rewiring anti-correlated to order; topological neighbourhoods reshape the flocking phase diagram; a Vicsek-type transition appears whose susceptibility peak grows with system size. One prediction failed and one subsumption claim remains unconfirmed.
conclusion: The GPS provides a unified metamodel whose structural components coordinatize a space of swarming and agent-based models, with the dependence of the interaction graph on state isolated as the key distinguishing feature between the two communities.

title: Lower Semicontinuity Of Dimension For quasi-Bernoulli Measures Under Conformal Projections
authors: Attila Losonczi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the dependence of the Hausdorff dimension of projected quasi-Bernoulli measures on a conformal iterated function system on the real line. For every fixed quasi-Bernoulli probability measure on the symbolic space, we prove that the dimension of its push-forward under the coding map is lower semicontinuous in the [MATH] topology, without any separation assumption or shift-invariance requirement on the symbolic measure. The proof combines bounded distortion and finite-scale entropy estimates with uniform control of the entropy dimension over measures whose densities are bounded above and below. For invariant Gibbs measures associated with H\"older continuous potentials, we also prove joint lower semicontinuity with respect to the defining system and the potential. As an application, we obtain a generic dimension formula: for each fixed shift-invariant quasi-Bernoulli measure, a dense [MATH] set of systems with derivative moduli strictly less than 1/2 has projected dimension equal to the minimum of one and the entropy-to-Lyapunov-exponent ratio.
tldr: The paper proves lower semicontinuity of the Hausdorff dimension of projected quasi-Bernoulli measures under conformal iterated function systems on the real line, including a generic dimension formula for shift-invariant Gibbs measures.
motivation: Understanding how the dimension of fractal measures behaves under projection and perturbation of the defining system is a central problem in geometric measure theory and conformal dynamics.
method: The proof combines bounded distortion estimates with finite-scale entropy estimates and uniform control of entropy dimension over measures with bounded densities; joint lower semicontinuity is established for Hölder Gibbs potentials.
result: Dimension of push-forward measures is lower semicontinuous in the L^1 topology without separation or shift-invariance assumptions, and for typical systems with derivative moduli below 1/2 the projected dimension equals min(1, entropy-to-Lyapunov ratio).
conclusion: The results extend semicontinuity and dimension-formula phenomena to broad classes of quasi-Bernoulli and Gibbs measures, with implications for generic dimension behavior in conformal repellers.

title: A Fast And Accurate Time-Space Decomposition For Unit Commitment With Storage
authors: Chance Brainard, Kylind Reagan, Shaked Regev
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Grid-scale batteries couple decisions across time. This makes unit commitment (UC) with thousands of buses, batteries, generators, and alternating current constraints intractable. We introduce a time-space decomposition (TSD) heuristic to solve the problem. We first calculate target net battery charge or discharge rates on a zonal level, relaxing spatial constraints. We then incorporate this target into the Relax-and-Round UC (RRUC) solver from our previous work. RRUC enforces the spatial transmission constraints and transfers power between zones, if that reduces costs. We show that our TSD produces an error of about 0.1% on a simpler economic dispatch problem with batteries. This is larger than the error produced by RRUC in the tests in our previous work. So, we conjecture that the combined error of our two approximations is not much larger than 0.1%. We show that TSD with RRUC can solve systems with 10,000 buses in about 6 minutes, with sub-quadratic scaling, making it suitable for real time operations on an ISO-sized system.
tldr: The paper introduces a time-space decomposition heuristic for solving large-scale unit commitment problems with grid-scale battery storage, achieving ~0.1% error and solving 10,000-bus systems in about six minutes.
motivation: Grid-scale batteries couple decisions across time, making unit commitment with thousands of buses, batteries, generators, and AC constraints computationally intractable for real-time ISO operations.
method: A two-stage time-space decomposition (TSD) heuristic first computes zonal target battery charge/discharge rates by relaxing spatial constraints, then embeds these targets into the authors' Relax-and-Round UC (RRUC) solver, which enforces transmission constraints and allows inter-zonal power transfers when cost-reducing.
result: TSD achieves about 0.1% error on a simpler economic dispatch problem with batteries, and combined with RRUC solves systems with 10,000 buses in roughly six minutes with sub-quadratic scaling.
conclusion: The approach is claimed suitable for real-time operation on ISO-sized systems, with the combined approximation error conjectured to be only slightly above 0.1%.

title: NeRI: Neural Residual Iteration For Elliptic Operator Equations And Variational Inequalities
authors: Jianfeng Ning Michael Hinterm\"uller
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18992v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we propose a so-called {\it Neural Residual Iteration} (NeRI), a weak-form neural-network framework for solving a class of elliptic operator equations and variational inequalities, including nonlinear and nonsymmetric problems that may not admit a global energy functional. The key idea is to construct, at each iteration, a state-dependent linear functional whose derivative with respect to the trial function recovers the current weak residual. A single gradient step is then performed on the residual, yielding a residual-driven neural update without requiring a global energy functional or an additional test network. From a function-space perspective, NeRI can be interpreted as a neural-tangent-kernel-preconditioned realization of classical residual iterations, thereby bridging classical iterative solvers and neural-network optimization. We further extend NeRI to elliptic variational inequalities (VIs) through penalized and constraint-preserving formulations. For wide two-layer networks under gradient flow, we prove finite-time lazy-training estimates and derive an [MATH]-error decomposition relative to the exact weak solution. Numerical experiments on several elliptic problems demonstrate the effectiveness of NeRI, particularly for nonsymmetric and low-regularity problems.
tldr: The paper introduces NeRI, a weak-form neural-network framework for solving elliptic operator equations and variational inequalities via residual-driven iterations that avoid requiring a global energy functional.
motivation: Many existing physics-informed or weak-form neural solvers rely on a global energy functional or an extra test network, which fails for nonlinear, nonsymmetric problems and variational inequalities.
method: At each iteration a state-dependent linear functional is constructed whose derivative in the trial function recovers the current weak residual; a single gradient step on this residual yields a neural update, interpretable as a neural-tangent-kernel-preconditioned classical residual iteration, extended to VIs via penalized and constraint-preserving formulations.
result: For wide two-layer networks under gradient flow the authors prove finite-time lazy-training estimates and an error decomposition relative to the exact weak solution, and numerical experiments show effectiveness on nonsymmetric and low-regularity elliptic problems.
conclusion: NeRI bridges classical iterative solvers and neural-network optimization, providing a functional-analytic framework for elliptic PDEs and variational inequalities without global energy functionals.

title: Delay Closure Of Observable Dynamics For The Heat Equation
authors: Xiaoting Han, Dongbin Xiu, Ludmil T. Zikatanov
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19040v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study finite-delay representations of point observables, which are solution values at selected spatial locations, for spatially discretized heat equations. We show that the observables satisfy closed dynamical systems whose evolution depends only on their own history, without requiring solution values elsewhere in the domain. Using semigroup properties, we analyze low-rank approximate closures that can use substantially fewer delay terms than the exact representation. We consider two computational approaches: direct least-squares fitting of delay coefficients from observable trajectories and shift-invert Krylov approximation of the semigroup using preconditioned linear solves. Numerical experiments for constant- and variable-coefficient heat equations in one, two, and three dimensions illustrate the effects of memory length and sensor information on prediction. The results are consistent with the theoretical analysis.
tldr: The paper derives finite-delay closed dynamical systems for point observables of spatially discretized heat equations and constructs low-rank approximate closures using least-squares fitting and shift-invert Krylov semigroup approximations.
motivation: Simulating or predicting the evolution of local observables in a large discretized PDE typically requires full-domain state information, which is computationally expensive; the authors ask whether observables alone can obey a self-contained memory-dependent dynamics.
method: Using semigroup theory, they prove exact closure of observable histories under finite delays, then build reduced closures via direct least-squares fitting of delay coefficients and preconditioned shift-invert Krylov approximation of the semigroup operator.
result: Numerical experiments on constant- and variable-coefficient heat equations in one, two, and three dimensions confirm the theoretical closure and quantify how memory length and sensor placement affect prediction accuracy with far fewer delay terms than the exact representation.
conclusion: Observable dynamics of diffusive systems admit compact delay-based closures, offering a practical reduced-order modeling route that avoids full-state reconstruction, consistent with the semigroup analysis.

title: Intersection Cuts For Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programs Via Decision-Diagram-Free Sets
authors: Danial Davarnia Junyuan Qiu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a novel decision-diagram-based framework for generating intersection cuts to strengthen polyhedral relaxations of bounded mixed-integer nonlinear programs (MINLPs) with general nonlinear constraints. Building on decision diagrams (DDs) that provide outer approximations of MINLP feasible regions, we propose the concept of DD-free sets, which are convex regions whose interiors do not intersect the sets represented by the DDs. By exploiting the underlying graphical structure, we develop efficient methods for constructing these regions without requiring restrictive assumptions on the functional form of nonlinear constraints or access to distance oracles. We investigate the maximality properties of DD-free sets and devise algorithms for obtaining maximal forbidden regions within several structured classes. The resulting intersection cuts exploit geometric information retained in DD representations, enabling further strengthening of relaxations beyond what can be achieved through conventional DD-based convexification. We also introduce interval DDs to facilitate the representation of general nonlinear constraints and establish convergence results for intersections of constraint-specific DDs, providing a theoretical foundation for their integration into global optimization frameworks. Computational experiments on challenging open instances from MINLPLib, encompassing a broad range of nonlinear and nonconvex structures, demonstrate that the proposed approach can substantially improve dual bounds and achieve greater optimality-gap closure than state-of-the-art global optimization solvers. These findings highlight the potential of exploiting graphical representations of infeasible regions to develop stronger cutting planes for general MINLPs.
tldr: The paper introduces a decision-diagram-based framework of DD-free sets to generate intersection cuts that strengthen polyhedral relaxations of bounded mixed-integer nonlinear programs.
motivation: Global solvers for MINLPs with general nonlinear constraints suffer from weak relaxations, and existing decision-diagram convexifications leave geometric information unexploited.
method: The authors define DD-free sets as convex regions whose interiors avoid the DD-represented outer approximation, develop constructive algorithms for maximal forbidden regions over structured classes, and introduce interval DDs to encode general nonlinear constraints.
result: Computational experiments on hard MINLPLib instances show substantial dual-bound improvements and greater optimality-gap closure than state-of-the-art global optimization solvers.
conclusion: Exploiting graphical representations of infeasible regions yields stronger cutting planes for general MINLPs, with convergence guarantees supporting integration into global optimization frameworks.

title: Agent-ZTA: A chain-Aware Zero Trust Model For Bidirectional Security-State Propagation And Runtime Containment In Multi-Agent Delegation
authors: Toqeer Ali Syed Asadullah Abdullah Khan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent systems increasingly delegate tasks and permissions across chains of autonomous agents that invoke protected tools. Although agent identities and delegated credentials may remain valid throughout a workflow, the security condition of any agent along the chain can deteriorate during runtime execution-either through upstream compromise or downstream ingestion of untrusted inputs. Authorization models based solely on the immediate caller and its static delegated scope fail to account for these mid-execution state changes. This paper develops Agent-ZTA, a chain-aware Zero Trust authorization and containment model that links runtime security-state changes across multi-agent delegation graphs. The model distinguishes an agent's path-specific delegated authority bound from the effective permissions currently exercisable under trusted policy. It defines an architecture featuring independently enforced policy decisions, authenticated delegation provenance, a dynamic chain-state view, and explicit fail-safe handling of missing or stale authorization signals. Furthermore, Agent-ZTA defines bidirectional security state propagation, allowing downstream security events to affect relevant upstream workflow states, and specifies adaptive branch-scoped containment through restricted permissions and a sandbox ("jail") execution mode where an isolation boundary is available. The deterministic decision procedure, five stated security properties, and worked authorization traces show how accepted security-state changes constrain affected operations while preserving original delegation bounds and separating unrelated workflow branches under the defined policies. Finally, the paper states its trust assumptions and the exact scope of its security properties.
tldr: Agent-ZTA is a chain-aware Zero Trust authorization and containment model for multi-agent delegation graphs that tracks runtime security-state changes across agent chains.
motivation: Static delegated credentials and caller-only authorization checks fail when an agent's security condition degrades mid-execution due to upstream compromise or ingestion of untrusted downstream inputs.
method: The authors formalize path-specific delegated authority bounds versus effective permissions, and specify an architecture with independently enforced policy decisions, authenticated delegation provenance, a dynamic chain-state view, fail-safe handling of stale signals, bidirectional state propagation, and branch-scoped containment via restricted permissions or sandboxed execution.
result: A deterministic decision procedure, five stated security properties, and worked authorization traces demonstrate that accepted security-state changes constrain affected operations while preserving delegation bounds and isolating unrelated workflow branches.
conclusion: The model provides explicit trust assumptions and a clearly scoped set of containment guarantees for securing multi-agent delegation workflows, though validation appears limited to formal traces rather than empirical deployment.

title: St-gat: A Leakage-Free Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Framework For Robust Network Intrusion Detection
authors: Nikhil Parkar, Sanskar Pandey, Siddhi Prajapati, Suganeshwari G, Syed Ibrahim
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intrusion detection systems are a central defence in modern networks. Deep learning models report strong anomaly-detection results, but evaluations on standard benchmarks such as CSE-CIC-IDS-2018 are often inflated by two methodological problems: temporal leakage from overlapping sliding windows, and contamination from preprocessing fitted before the train/test split. Per-flow classifiers also ignore the spatio-temporal dependencies across sequences of network flows. We propose a Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Network (ST-GAT) that represents traffic as a sequence of graph snapshots. It builds k-Nearest Neighbour (k-NN) edges within each window, applies multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) layers for spatial aggregation, and uses a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network with temporal attention for sequence modelling. To prevent leakage, we use non-overlapping temporal windows (stride equal to window length) and fit all preprocessing on the training split only. We compare three class-imbalance strategies: inverse class-frequency weighting, dynamic balanced sampling, and few-shot metric prototyping. Across three random seeds, ST-GAT with inverse class weighting reached a Macro-F1 of 96.65% (+/- 0.87) and an accuracy of 99.14%. This is 14.3 percentage points higher in Macro-F1 than a per-flow Random Forest baseline (82.34%). Balanced sampling reduced Macro-F1 by 2.3 points (to 94.37%) relative to loss weighting. This suggests that aggressive resampling of small, noisy minority classes can hurt detection in heavily imbalanced traffic.
tldr: ST-GAT is a spatio-temporal graph attention framework for network intrusion detection that eliminates temporal leakage and preprocessing contamination in benchmark evaluations.
motivation: Existing deep-learning intrusion detectors report inflated results on benchmarks like CSE-CIC-IDS-2018 due to overlapping sliding windows and preprocessing fitted before the train/test split, and per-flow classifiers ignore cross-flow spatio-temporal dependencies.
method: Traffic is modeled as a sequence of graph snapshots with k-NN edges within non-overlapping windows, aggregated by multi-head Graph Attention layers, then sequenced with a BiLSTM plus temporal attention; three class-imbalance strategies are compared.
result: With inverse class weighting, ST-GAT achieves 96.65% (+/- 0.87) Macro-F1 and 99.14% accuracy across three seeds, 14.3 points above a per-flow Random Forest baseline (82.34%); balanced sampling degrades Macro-F1 by 2.3 points.
conclusion: Leakage-free evaluation and spatio-temporal graph modeling substantially improve intrusion detection, and aggressive resampling of small noisy minority classes can be counterproductive in heavily imbalanced traffic.

title: Veto Proportionality In Multiwinner Voting With Ranked Preferences
authors: Haris Aziz, Yuhang Guo, Patrick Lederer
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proportional representation in committee voting with ranked preferences requires voter groups to influence the selected committee in proportion to their size. Existing axioms, such as proportionality for solid coalitions (PSC), demand that like-minded groups of voters are entitled to elect a fair number of candidates to the committee. However, in applications where voters are collectively affected by the entire committee, it may be equally important that no group is confronted with a disproportionate number of candidates that it regards as undesirable. Motivated by this, we initiate the study of veto proportionality in committee elections with ranked preferences. Our central notion, the proportional multiwinner veto core (PMVC), generalizes Moulin's proportional singlewinner veto core to multiwinner elections by allowing groups of voters to partially veto sets of candidates. We analyze how the PMVC relates to existing fairness notions and design rules that are guaranteed to select committees from the PMVC. Specifically, we first introduce a duality framework that connects inclusion- and exclusion-based fairness notions and show, e.g., that the dual axiom of the PMVC strengthens PSC. We further show that STV satisfies the dual axiom of the PMVC, which also implies the existence of committees in the PMVC. Subject to a strengthening of committee monotonicity, we characterize the rules that always return committees in the PMVC as sequential adaptations of singlewinner voting rules that always select from the proportional singlewinner veto core. By our duality framework, this also gives rise to a new class of rules that satisfy PSC. We further prove that the dual axiom of the PMVC and RankPJR+ are jointly satisfiable, thereby pushing the frontier of fairness guarantees that can always be attained. Finally, we show that deciding whether a given committee belongs to the PMVC is coNP-complete.
tldr: The paper introduces veto proportionality for multiwinner committee elections with ranked preferences, centered on the proportional multiwinner veto core (PMVC).
motivation: Existing proportionality axioms such as PSC ensure groups can elect candidates in proportion to their size, but in settings where voters are affected by the whole committee it also matters that no group faces a disproportionate number of undesirable candidates.
method: The authors axiomatize the PMVC, develop a duality framework linking inclusion- and exclusion-based fairness notions, and analyze which voting rules (e.g., STV, sequential adaptations of single-winner rules) always return committees in the PMVC.
result: They show the dual axiom of PMVC strengthens PSC, that STV satisfies this dual axiom (implying PMVC non-emptiness), characterize PMVC-returning rules under strengthened committee monotonicity, prove joint satisfiability with RankPJR+, and show PMVC membership testing is coNP-complete.
conclusion: The work pushes the frontier of attainable fairness guarantees in committee voting and yields a new class of PSC-satisfying rules via duality.

title: Agent Authenticator: Passkey-Grade, Hardware-Bound Authentication For Ai Agents
authors: Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19536v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding agents now push code, publish packages, call model APIs and operate cloud resources on behalf of developers. They authenticate to these services with the same bearer secrets humans use, personal access tokens, API keys and package-registry tokens, stored where the model, its subprocesses and any co-resident malware can read them. Incidents in 2025 and 2026, including prompt-injection attacks on coding agents and self-propagating supply-chain worms, show that this arrangement fails in predictable ways. Passkeys solved the analogous problem for humans, but they require a human gesture on every use and cannot be operated by an autonomous process. We present the Agent Authenticator, a design that gives agents passkey-grade authentication properties: per-service hardware-bound keys, no shared secrets, origin binding enforced by the runtime rather than the model, normalized attestation of the execution environment, human-signed scoped mandates, and cross-device human approval for high-risk actions. The same protocol serves agents on developer laptops and in cloud enclaves, and it deploys as a profile over existing mechanisms, MCP authorization, OAuth token exchange including the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant, git and SSH, rather than as a new identity system. The authenticator also produces a signed, hash-chained record of each action it authorizes. We analyze the design against a threat model centered on prompt injection and same-host compromise, map it onto five documented incidents, and discuss its limits.
tldr: The paper proposes the Agent Authenticator, a passkey-style, hardware-bound authentication protocol for autonomous AI agents that avoids shared bearer secrets and enforces origin binding and human-signed mandates outside the model.
motivation: AI coding agents currently authenticate to services using bearer secrets (API keys, tokens) that are readable by the model, its subprocesses, and co-resident malware, leading to documented prompt-injection and supply-chain attacks; human passkeys cannot be used because they require a per-use human gesture.
method: The authors present a design that provides per-service hardware-bound keys, runtime-enforced origin binding, normalized attestation of the execution environment, human-signed scoped mandates, cross-device approval for high-risk actions, and hash-chained signed action logs, deployed as a profile over MCP authorization, OAuth token exchange (Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant), git and SSH.
result: The design is analyzed against a threat model centered on prompt injection and same-host compromise, mapped onto five documented incidents, and its limitations are discussed; no formal security proof or implementation benchmark is reported.
conclusion: Agent Authenticator offers a practical, deployable authentication layer giving agents passkey-grade properties, but it remains a systems-security design outside the scope of quantum information science.

title: TrustBound: Mechanized Completeness For Payment Epochs Initiated By Ai Agents
authors: Sandip Nandi, Aishwarya Bose, Apurba Bose, Soovadeep Bakshi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19551v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Payment operations requested by an AI agent may remain executable, or their outcomes unresolved, after the agent has stopped. We study when a trusted payment service can account for every payment in an epoch and exclude further payments under earlier authority. We give a Lean model in which operations are recorded before they receive execution authority and both actions are serialized with an admission fence. We prove that fencing fixes a journal that covers every modeled effect and outstanding right; that discharging those rights prevents further effects; and that truthful outcomes for the recorded identities then give exact accounting. A provider-contract model, mapped to the admission model, makes created payment objects inert until registered. Premise-removal mutations confirm that each key premise is needed. We connect the models to an executable service: six service histories are checked against the model in Lean, and bounded schedules, scripted clients and concurrent workers exercise its reconciliation. The concurrent experiments uncovered a conflict caused by reordered provider reads, which serializing retrieval with journal updates removes in all tested cases. The result separates two obligations that are easily conflated in practice - preventing future payments and accounting for past ones - and states precisely which service guarantees establish each.
tldr: TrustBound presents a Lean-mechanized model of payment epochs initiated by AI agents, proving that admission fencing and journal recording together guarantee exact accounting of past payments and exclusion of future ones.
motivation: Payments requested by an AI agent can remain executable or unresolved after the agent halts, creating a gap between preventing future payments and accounting for past ones that practitioners often conflate.
method: The authors build a Lean formalization in which operations are journaled before receiving execution authority and both steps are serialized by an admission fence, plus a provider-contract model mapped onto it, validated with premise-removal mutations and an executable service tested against six service histories and concurrent schedules.
result: The proofs show fencing yields a journal covering every modeled effect and outstanding right, discharging rights blocks further effects, and truthful outcomes give exact accounting; concurrent experiments revealed a reconciliation conflict from reordered provider reads that serializing retrieval with journal updates removed in all tested cases.
conclusion: The work cleanly separates the obligations of preventing future payments from accounting for past ones and specifies which service guarantees establish each, though it lies entirely outside quantum information science.

title: Coalgebra For True Concurrency
authors: Yong Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give the coalgebra for true concurrency along the way paved by traditional coalgebra based on bisimulation. This coalgebra is based on truly concurrent bisimulation, and we give its definition and a simple truly concurrent process algebra.
tldr: The paper develops a coalgebraic framework for true concurrency, defining truly concurrent bisimulation and a simple truly concurrent process algebra.
motivation: Traditional coalgebra is built on (interleaving) bisimulation, which cannot faithfully capture truly concurrent behaviour; the author aims to extend the coalgebraic method to the truly concurrent setting.
method: A coalgebra based on truly concurrent bisimulation is defined, together with the corresponding notion of bisimulation and a simple truly concurrent process algebra presented along traditional coalgebraic lines.
result: A definitional foundation for truly concurrent coalgebra and an associated process algebra are given, establishing the basic theory in analogy with standard coalgebra.
conclusion: The work extends coalgebraic semantics from interleaving to true concurrency, providing groundwork for further theory of truly concurrent processes.

title: HalluProbe: Exploiting Vlm Hallucinations For Backdoor Detection
authors: Ji Guo, Xiaolong Qin, Jin Jiang, Yijing Liu, Pei Ke, Aiguo Chen, Wenbo Jiang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks introduced through data poisoning, making effective backdoor detection a critical security challenge. In this paper, we uncover a novel connection between VLM hallucinations and backdoor behaviors and exploit this connection for backdoor detection. Our key insight is that poisoned training data induces strong language priors toward the backdoor target token, while such priors are also a major source of hallucinations. This suggests that enhancing hallucinations can expose hidden backdoor-related priors. Specifically, backdoored VLMs tend to hallucinate backdoor target tokens more frequently across diverse inputs, while the hallucinated tokens of clean VLMs are largely random and exhibit no stable target-specific bias. Based on this observation, we propose HalluProbe, which enhances hallucinations during output decoding and measures the distributional consistency of hallucinated tokens to identify backdoored VLMs. We evaluate HalluProbe against six representative VLM backdoor attacks across three models. Experimental results demonstrate that HalluProbe can effectively detect backdoored VLMs with an accuracy exceeding 90%, outperforming existing backdoor detection methods.
tldr: HalluProbe detects backdoors in vision-language models by amplifying hallucination during decoding and measuring the consistency of hallucinated tokens toward the backdoor target.
motivation: Backdoor attacks via data poisoning are a serious security threat to VLMs, and existing detection methods are inadequate; the authors observe that the language priors causing hallucinations also underlie backdoor behavior.
method: The approach enhances hallucination during output decoding and then measures the distributional consistency of hallucinated tokens across diverse inputs, flagging models whose hallucinations concentrate on a stable target token rather than being random.
result: Evaluated against six representative VLM backdoor attacks on three models, HalluProbe detects backdoored models with over 90% accuracy, outperforming existing detection baselines.
conclusion: Exploiting the link between hallucination and backdoor priors yields an effective, model-agnostic backdoor detection method for VLMs.

title: Cheri Under Fault Injection: An Emulation-Based Security Evaluation Of Capability Hardware Enhanced Risc Instructions
authors: Eva Sophia Schreyer
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19915v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory-safety vulnerabilities continue to dominate real-world exploit chains despite decades of research into software mitigations. CHERI is a hardware architecture that enforces spatial and temporal memory safety by augmenting pointers with hardware-checked metadata, thus preventing software-based exploitation, but its threat model explicitly excludes fault injection. This thesis investigates whether targeted fault injection can undermine CHERI's memory-safety guarantees in a pure-capability CHERI-RISC-V environment. Two fault classes are considered: bit flips corrupting capability metadata, and fault-induced check skipping on capability store instructions. We implement fault injection primitives in a QEMU-based emulation environment, which enables deterministic, repeatable experiments without specialised hardware. With them, we demonstrate four attack scenarios: buffer overflows, control-flow hijacking, data-only attacks, and use-after-free. Each succeeds with one or two targeted faults (lower bounds under the emulation-based setting). Check skipping offers an alternative route to control-flow hijacking and data-only attacks, with a minimum of one fault. These results show that CHERI's guarantees depend on the physical integrity of capability metadata, the uninterrupted execution of metadata checks, and the integrity of the revocation bitmap: a single targeted fault can circumvent spatial safety, temporal safety, or control-flow integrity. CHERI still raises the cost of exploitation, since fault injection is a prerequisite for every attack and the sentry mechanism forces an attacker to supply a valid tagged capability or spend a second fault restoring the tag. Based on these findings, we propose mitigations: ECC-protected capability memory, capability field authentication codes, redundant execution of security-critical checks, and revocation bitmap integrity verification.
tldr: An emulation-based study showing that targeted fault injection into capability metadata can defeat CHERI-RISC-V memory-safety guarantees.
motivation: CHERI provides hardware-enforced spatial and temporal memory safety, but its threat model explicitly excludes fault injection, leaving open whether physical faults can undermine its guarantees.
