method: The author implements deterministic fault-injection primitives in a QEMU-based CHERI-RISC-V emulator, injecting bit flips into capability metadata and skipping capability-check instructions.
result: Four attack classes (buffer overflow, control-flow hijacking, data-only attacks, use-after-free) each succeed with one or two targeted faults, showing that capability tag integrity, check execution, and revocation bitmap integrity are all single-fault breakable.
conclusion: CHERI still raises exploitation cost, and the thesis proposes ECC-protected capability memory, field authentication codes, redundant checks, and revocation-bitmap verification as mitigations.

title: Sparse Rotatable Arrays (SRAs) For Cell-Free Mimo: Network-Wide Design Of Antenna Activation And Panel Orientation
authors: Ailing Zheng, Qingqing Wu, Xiyuan Liu, Wei Feng, Wen Chen, Guoying Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates a sparse rotatable array (SRA)-enabled cell-free multiuser multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system. Under a network-wide antenna activation budget, distributed access points (APs) select active antenna elements from their installed arrays and adjust panel orientations, enabling joint control of sparse array apertures and antenna directivity. To avoid frequent hardware reconfiguration in response to instantaneous channel variations, we formulate a two-timescale stochastic optimization problem to maximize the expected minimum-user rate. Long-term antenna activation and panel orientations are optimized based on user spatial distributions and statistical channel state information (CSI), while short-term precoders adapt to instantaneous CSI. Under line-of-sight (LoS) propagation, we derive the optimal single-user antenna allocation, characterize the two-user max-min signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) and establish conditions for discrete activation and panel rotation to attain the continuous-position benchmark, and obtain a closed-form multi-AP zero-forcing (ZF) allocation benchmark under a continuous antenna-count relaxation. For the general mixed-integer nonconvex stochastic problem, we develop an alternating algorithm based on sample-average approximation (SAA), integrating uplink-downlink (UL-DL) duality for short-term precoding, weighted minimum mean-square error (WMMSE) surrogates for panel-orientation optimization, and multi-start greedy search for antenna activation. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed design outperforms the fixed-array benchmark, improves all-user service reliability with fewer active antennas, and adapts effectively to nonuniform user spatial distributions.
tldr: The paper designs sparse rotatable arrays for cell-free multiuser MIMO systems, jointly optimizing antenna activation and panel orientation across the network via a two-timescale stochastic optimization framework.
motivation: Frequent hardware reconfiguration in response to instantaneous channel variations is impractical, and existing fixed-array architectures do not exploit joint control of sparse apertures and antenna directivity to improve worst-case user rate under nonuniform user distributions.
method: A two-timescale stochastic optimization problem maximizing expected minimum-user rate is formulated, with long-term antenna activation and panel orientations optimized from statistical CSI and short-term precoders adapting to instantaneous CSI; an alternating algorithm combining UL-DL duality, WMMSE surrogates, and multi-start greedy search over sample-average approximation is developed, alongside analytical characterizations under LoS propagation.
result: Analytical results include optimal single-user antenna allocation, two-user max-min SINR characterization with conditions for discrete activation and rotation to match the continuous-position benchmark, and a closed-form multi-AP ZF allocation benchmark; numerics show gains over fixed-array baselines with fewer active antennas and reliable adaptation to nonuniform user distributions.
conclusion: SRA-enabled cell-free MIMO with joint activation and orientation control offers an effective, hardware-friendly means of improving network-wide service reliability, though the work is purely classical wireless communication engineering.

title: Security Of Deep Research Agents: Attack Surface, Defenses, Benchmarks, And Agenda Seeding Against Research Planning
authors: Yang Luo (peking University), Guangpu Chen (peking University), Yichen Liu (peking University), Zhaoyu Chen (peking University), Yifeng Gao (peking University), Zhiyang Ding (peking University), Qingni Shen (peking University), Zhonghai Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.20045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep research and agentic search agents autonomously retrieve content from the open web and generate reports with citations, and their outputs are often taken directly as research conclusions. This paper systematizes security research in this area along four stages, namely retrieval, planning, evidence integration, and report generation. We present a unified threat model, a taxonomy of attacks and defenses, and a review of evaluation benchmarks, and we align the area dimension by dimension with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) poisoning, prompt injection, and generative engine optimization (GEO). Coding 34 primary studies shows that only 26.5% of them involve the planning stage, and none performs an end-to-end poisoning evaluation on commercial products. To address this gap, we propose the agenda seeding attack, in which the attacker writes no instructions and only introduces a fictitious evaluation metric. Across 3,520 sandboxed research runs under the same budget, GEO and prompt injection are nearly ineffective, whereas agenda seeding makes the attacker's target the top pick in 16% to 28% of reports. Injection detection and query anchoring fail against it, verification prompting hurts utility, and our proposed provenance tagging preserves utility but can be bypassed by multi-site bait. Finally, we propose eight research directions.
tldr: This paper systematizes the security of LLM-based deep research agents and proposes a novel 'agenda seeding' poisoning attack that subtly steers which sources an agent cites.
motivation: Agentic deep-research systems scrape the open web and their reports are often treated as authoritative conclusions, creating an attack surface (retrieval, planning, evidence integration, report generation) that has not been systematically studied.
method: The authors build a unified threat model and taxonomy across four pipeline stages, review 34 primary studies and benchmarks, align the area with RAG poisoning, prompt injection, and generative engine optimization, then run 3,520 sandboxed research runs comparing attacks and defenses.
result: GEO and prompt injection are nearly ineffective, but agenda seeding—inserting only a fictitious evaluation metric—makes the attacker's target the top recommendation in 16–28% of reports; injection detection and query anchoring fail, verification prompting harms utility, and provenance tagging is only partially effective.
conclusion: Planning-stage manipulation is an under-studied and potent attack surface for research agents, and the authors outline eight open research directions toward robust defenses.

title: Sequential Semantic-Non-Semantic Watermarking: Robustness Against UnMarker Attacks
authors: Md Ifraham Iqbal
abstract: ArXiv:2611.20115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have accelerated digital content generation and intensified concerns around fraud, misuse, counterfeiting, and content provenance. Defensive image watermarking provides a practical mechanism for identifying and tracing digital content, but recent watermark-removal attacks challenge its robustness. This study investigates Sequential Semantic Non-Semantic Watermarking (SSNSW), which combines HiDDeN and StegaStamp as complementary non-semantic and semantic watermarking schemes. Using 50 images from MS-COCO and CelebA-HQ, both embedding orders are evaluated, followed by UnMarker's non-semantic and semantic attacks applied individually and sequentially. Results show that both watermarks remain highly decodable after dual embedding, with only limited embedding-order effects. Under individual attacks, one watermark generally remains strongly decodable: StegaStamp under the non-semantic attack and HiDDeN under the semantic attack. Sequential attacks are therefore required to substantially reduce both watermark signals, while attack order has a limited and configuration-dependent effect. The semantic attack also shows a broader effect across the two watermark types than the non-semantic attack. LPIPS remains relatively low in several settings, although qualitative inspection reveals noticeable distortions, particularly in selected facial images, indicating that LPIPS should not be used alone to assess visual quality. Overall, the findings show that combining complementary watermark types can increase robustness against single-stage removal attacks and motivate broader multi-layer watermarking, stronger perceptual evaluation, and further study of sequential watermark-removal strategies.
tldr: The paper evaluates a sequential dual image-watermarking scheme (HiDDeN plus StegaStamp) and shows that complementary semantic and non-semantic watermarks improve robustness against UnMarker removal attacks.
motivation: AI-generated content raises provenance and misuse concerns, and existing defensive image watermarks are vulnerable to learned watermark-removal attacks, motivating layered watermarking strategies.
method: Fifty images from MS-COCO and CelebA-HQ are watermarked with HiDDeN and StegaStamp in both embedding orders, then subjected to UnMarker's non-semantic and semantic attacks individually and sequentially, with decoding rates and LPIPS measured.
result: Both watermarks remain highly decodable after dual embedding; single attacks typically leave one watermark intact, so sequential attacks are needed to degrade both, and the semantic attack affects both watermark types more broadly than the non-semantic one.
conclusion: Combining complementary watermark types increases robustness to single-stage removal attacks, motivating multi-layer watermarking, stronger perceptual metrics than LPIPS alone, and further study of sequential removal attacks.

title: Power Scaling Across Link Utilization With Gpam-4 Signaling And Event-Driven Reception
authors: Maya Mekel, Jeries Mattar, Nicolas Wainstein
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work highlights the potential of combining event-based signaling with event-driven reception to achieve receiver power scaling across link utilization, without requiring wake-up, locking, or data-rate reconfiguration. The approach is demonstrated using the proposed four-level Gaussian pulse-amplitude modulation (GPAM-4) scheme and a corresponding event-driven receiver. By employing a resettable ring voltage-controlled oscillator (RRVCO) as its front end, the receiver achieves inherently event-driven symbol measurement, initiated directly by each received pulse. Symbols are decoded directly from the final RRVCO phase state, eliminating a counter-based back end. Simulated in 28-nm CMOS, the receiver power is evaluated across a [MATH] range of effective data rates---from 0.15 mW at the peak rate of 8 Gb/s, down to 2.5 [MATH]W under active/idle operation and 1.6 [MATH]W under data rate change at 80 Mb/s. The receiver thus achieves power reductions of [MATH] and [MATH], while its energy per bit increases by only [MATH] and [MATH], respectively.
tldr: The paper presents a GPAM-4 signaling scheme with an event-driven receiver that scales power with link utilization in 28-nm CMOS.
motivation: The work aims to reduce receiver power across effective data rates without wake-up, locking, or data-rate reconfiguration.
method: It combines four-level Gaussian pulse-amplitude modulation with a resettable ring VCO front end that performs event-driven symbol measurement and decodes symbols from the final oscillator phase.
result: Simulations show receiver power from 0.15 mW at 8 Gb/s down to 2.5 µW in active/idle operation and 1.6 µW under data-rate change at 80 Mb/s, with modest energy-per-bit penalties.
conclusion: Event-based signaling and event-driven reception can provide useful power scaling in classical high-speed links, but the work is unrelated to quantum information science.

title: Community Odour Reports As A Forecastable Sensor Of Fugitive Emissions
authors: Timothy C. Pearce, David J. T. Smith, Alec Dobney, Alessia Freddo
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ambient air quality monitors (AAQMs) measure exposure to emissions from waste facilities at few points; for most residents the only record is their own odour reports, used by regulators as evidence of impact but not typically as measurements of exposure. Calibrated public reports are accepted measurements in seismology, but whether community odour reports can serve as a sensor of exposure, and be forecast, is untested against independent monitors. Here we show they can, at a UK landfill, with SENTINEL, which combines the public weather forecast, run through a dispersion model, with the reports already received and no instrument at the site. Judged against the independent monitors, monthly report frequency was correlated with hydrogen sulphide (r = 0.92) and daily reports remained associated with it beyond weather; they fell fourteenfold after a change at the source while modelled transport did not; and, with no gas data as input, gave exposure in both monitored postcodes within a factor of three of that measured. SENTINEL forecast daily report counts with skill 0.64 one day and 0.50 four days ahead, exceeding damped persistence four days ahead; the one-day gain over persistence was unresolved. Community odour reports can act as a relative sensor complementing sparse monitoring; a monitor is needed for absolute scale.
tldr: Community odour reports at a UK landfill, combined with weather forecasts and a dispersion model (SENTINEL), can act as a forecastable relative sensor of hydrogen sulphide exposure.
motivation: Ambient air quality monitors are sparse, so residents' odour reports are the main record of exposure but are not normally treated as quantitative measurements; the authors ask whether such reports can serve as a calibrated, forecastable sensor.
method: SENTINEL combines public weather forecasts run through a dispersion model with already-received community odour reports, requiring no on-site instrument, and is validated against independent AAQM hydrogen sulphide measurements using correlation, regression and forecast-skill analysis.
result: Monthly report frequency correlated strongly with H2S (r = 0.92), daily reports remained associated with H2S beyond weather, reports fell fourteenfold after a source change while modelled transport did not, and exposure estimates fell within a factor of three of measurements in both monitored postcodes; forecast skill was 0.64 at one day and 0.50 at four days.
conclusion: Community odour reports can serve as a relative exposure sensor complementing sparse monitoring, though a co-located monitor is still needed to fix the absolute scale.

title: How To Agree Without Agreeing
authors: Maria Kleshnina Casper van Elteren
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Consensus lets institutions decide without a central authority, but a record of agreement reveals neither its basis nor its credibility. We model support, standing aside and veto as responses to a proposal. A proposal can pass without active support, and the member least willing to allow passage limits what can be adopted, however many members oppose the proposal. Letting proposers moderate their demands can ease agreement while undermining the prescribed punishment. Proposal restrictions or deviation costs can preserve that threat. Across the initialisations tested, learning agents agree frequently even though many reconstructed rules allow profitable departures. In our sample of Antarctic Treaty working papers, 80% of proposals revising existing arrangements were adopted at submission, against 38% of new proposals. Consensus can keep producing agreement on what already exists while new protection waits.
tldr: A game-theoretic and agent-based model of consensus decision-making with support, abstention and veto options, applied to Antarctic Treaty working papers.
motivation: Institutions rely on consensus without central authority, yet a recorded agreement reveals neither its basis nor its credibility; the authors want to understand how veto power and proposal moderation shape what can be adopted.
method: The authors model responses to proposals (support, standing aside, veto) formally, study how proposer moderation and deviation costs affect the punishment threat, and run learning-agent simulations; they also code a sample of Antarctic Treaty working papers by proposal type.
result: Learning agents agree frequently even though many reconstructed rules permit profitable departures, and in the sampled working papers 80% of proposals revising existing arrangements were adopted at submission versus 38% of new proposals.
conclusion: Consensus procedures tend to reproduce agreement on what already exists while new protections stall, so proposal restrictions or deviation costs are needed to preserve credible threats.

title: Zariski Topology Of (Krasner) Hypermodules
authors: Behnam Afshar, Reza Ameri, Hashem Bordbar
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18726v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be a commutative Krasner hyperring with identity and [MATH] an [MATH]-hypermodule. We consider the prime spectrum [MATH], consisting of all prime subhypermodules of [MATH]. In this paper, we introduce a Zariski topology on [MATH] and investigate its fundamental topological properties, including irreducibility, connectedness, compactness, and separation axioms, providing necessary and sufficient conditions for each. In particular, we prove that [MATH] is irreducible if and only if the nilradical of [MATH] is a prime hyperideal, and that it is connected precisely when the underlying hyperring is not a nontrivial direct product. We further investigate the functoriality of the Zariski topology in the category of Krasner hyperrings and hypermodules. Moreover, using the fundamental relation [MATH], the smallest regular relation on [MATH] for which the quotient [MATH] becomes an [MATH]-module, we establish a correspondence between the Zariski topologies of [MATH] and [MATH]. We show that this correspondence is functorial and thereby relate the hypermodule-theoretic setting to the classical theory of modules over rings.
tldr: The paper introduces and studies a Zariski topology on the prime spectrum of prime subhypermodules of a Krasner hypermodule, characterizing irreducibility, connectedness, compactness and separation, and relating it to classical module theory via the fundamental relation.
motivation: Algebraic geometry-style spectra and Zariski topologies have proven powerful for rings and modules; the authors aim to extend this machinery to the more general setting of Krasner hyperrings and hypermodules.
method: They define the prime spectrum of prime subhypermodules, endow it with a Zariski topology, and analyze topological properties (irreducibility, connectedness, compactness, separation axioms), proving characterizations via the nilradical and direct-product decompositions; functoriality and a correspondence through the fundamental relation are also established.
result: The spectrum is shown to be irreducible iff the nilradical is a prime hyperideal, and connected precisely when the underlying hyperring is not a nontrivial direct product; the Zariski topologies of the hypermodule and of the quotient module via the fundamental relation are shown to correspond functorially.
conclusion: The work connects hypermodule-theoretic spectra to the classical theory of modules over rings, providing a topological framework for hyperalgebraic structures.

title: An Ode To Changing Variables: $v = Y/x$ Is For Victory
authors: Joseph Kraisler, Kayla S. Miller, Steven J. Miller
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most first courses in differential equations introduce students to very special differential equations which can be solved in closed form from a small set of techniques (such as separable equations and integrating factors). Frequently other equations can be converted to one of these forms through a change of variable; however, these transformations are usually just given without any explanation of people found them, or problems of these forms have nice solutions, but not related ones. We consider the first order differential equation [MATH] where [MATH] does not factor as [MATH], and assume [MATH] for some nice function [MATH] and some real number [MATH]. This can be reduced to a separable equation only when [MATH]. We then discuss generalizations and what conditions on [MATH] lead to a change of variables yielding a separable equation. Our goals are twofold. First, to encourage students and instructors to be active, questioning the methods and results, seeing how far they can be extended and why they work. Second, we discuss how to appropriately use AI to take ideas and special cases as prompts and quickly create extensions and editable notes that can be shared with students, freeing up professors (and students) from straightforward calculations sacrificing learning and understanding.
tldr: A pedagogical note on when first-order differential equations of the form y' = M(x,y) without factorization can be made separable via the substitution v = Y/x, plus advice on using AI to generate such extensions.
motivation: The authors want to demystify why particular change-of-variable tricks work, encourage students and instructors to question and extend textbook methods, and show how AI can be used responsibly to produce worked examples and notes.
method: They analyze first-order ODEs where M(x,y) does not factor, assume Y = f(x,y) with a scaling structure, derive the condition under which v = Y/x yields a separable equation, and then explore generalizations and conditions on f.
result: The reduction to a separable equation succeeds only under a specific condition on the scaling exponent, and the authors characterize classes of f admitting such substitutions.
conclusion: The work serves as a teaching device for active mathematical inquiry and as a case study in leveraging AI to extend special-case reasoning into shareable instructional material.

title: Averaged-Cost Control With Shared Feedback Under Model Uncertainty
authors: Piernicola Bettiol, Daisuke Inoue, Mat\'ias G\'omez-Aedo, Dante Kalise, Richard B. Vinter
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the shared-feedback design problem for finite-horizon averaged-cost control under model uncertainty represented by a joint law over the model parameter and initial state. One feedback map is shared across all realizations and uses only time and the current state as online inputs. We develop two methods: the nonlinear adjoint method combines forward closed-loop solves, backward adjoints, and joint-law policy gradients, while the linear moment method gives exact cost and gradient formulas for a homogeneous linear-quadratic design model by propagating conditional second moments. Numerical studies compare averaged and nominal designs for time-dependent neural feedback and static linear feedback in nonlinear Van der Pol and Stuart-Landau systems; the static gains are designed from oscillator linearizations and evaluated on the original nonlinear systems. Averaged design has lower cost in most comparisons.
tldr: The paper develops adjoint- and moment-based methods for designing a single shared state-feedback controller for finite-horizon averaged-cost control problems under joint parameter/initial-state uncertainty.
motivation: Shared-feedback design is hard because one feedback map must serve all realizations of an uncertain model, requiring optimization over a joint law rather than a nominal parameter.
method: A nonlinear adjoint method combining forward closed-loop solves, backward adjoints and joint-law policy gradients, plus a linear moment method giving exact cost and gradient formulas for a homogeneous linear-quadratic model via conditional second moments.
result: Numerical studies on Van der Pol and Stuart-Landau oscillators show averaged designs generally yield lower cost than nominal designs for both neural and static linear feedback.
conclusion: Averaged-cost design that accounts for model uncertainty can outperform nominal control design, with the two proposed methods providing tractable gradient-based tools.

title: Learning-Enhanced Reduce-Repair-Refine-Optimize Framework For Real-Time Train Platforming
authors: Md Tabish Haque, Sebastian Sehmisch, Christopher Szymula, Nikola Be\v{s}inovi\'c
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-time train platforming under disruptions requires rapid revision of routing, platforming, and timing decisions. Dense traffic and shared infrastructure create tightly coupled conflicts, making real-time optimization computationally demanding. This paper proposes a learning-enhanced Reduce-Repair-Refine-Optimize framework that reduces and selectively relaxes the routing search space to balance computational efficiency, feasibility, and solution quality. The reduction stage constructs a restricted MILP by fixing selected routing decisions using route-specific predictive models and thresholds, thereby accounting for heterogeneity across routes. Two adaptive mechanisms subsequently modify the reduced search space: repair selectively releases route fixings to restore feasibility, while refinement releases additional fixings to recover routing alternatives and improve solution quality without reverting to the unrestricted problem. Computational experiments on real-life disrupted station-area instances show that the framework matches or improves upon a recent rTPP heuristic in more than 80% of instances within 60~s. Under the common 180~s budget, the framework obtains strictly better terminal incumbents than the unrestricted MILP in 56.7% of all instances and 77.4% of hard instances. Moreover, it obtains better terminal incumbents than an otherwise identical variant without refinement in 71.9% of hard instances. The results demonstrate that learning-based search-space reduction is most effective when the reduced search space remains adaptable during optimization, enabling high-quality feasible solutions within the real-time computation budget.
tldr: A learning-enhanced reduce-repair-refine-optimize framework is proposed to solve real-time train platforming problems under disruptions by shrinking and adaptively relaxing the routing search space of a MILP.
motivation: Real-time train platforming under dense traffic and shared infrastructure produces tightly coupled conflicts that make exact optimization too slow for real-time budgets, so heuristic search-space reduction is needed.
method: Route-specific predictive models and thresholds fix selected routing decisions to build a restricted MILP; repair and refinement stages then selectively release fixings to restore feasibility and recover routing alternatives.
result: On real disrupted station-area instances the framework matches or beats a recent rTPP heuristic in over 80% of cases within 60 s, and yields better terminal incumbents than unrestricted MILP in 56.7% of all and 77.4% of hard instances under a 180 s budget.
conclusion: Learning-based search-space reduction works best when the reduced space stays adaptable during optimization, enabling high-quality feasible solutions within real-time limits.

title: Veech Dichotomy For Specific Covering Surface Over Veech Surface
authors: Haoran Hu
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19243v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is known that Veech dichotomy, which states that minimal directions are uniquely ergodic, holds for Veech surface and covering surface branched at a single non-periodic connection point of Veech surface. We give a sufficient condition for Veech dichotomy holds for a finite translation cover of a Veech surface, and applies it on branched cover of square-tiled surfaces to construct examples that satisfy Veech dichotomy but aren't Veech surfaces.
tldr: The paper gives a sufficient condition for the Veech dichotomy to hold for finite translation covers of Veech surfaces, and uses it to construct branched covers of square-tiled surfaces that satisfy the dichotomy without being Veech surfaces.
motivation: The Veech dichotomy (unique ergodicity of minimal directions) is known for Veech surfaces and for covers branched at a single non-periodic connection point, but a general criterion for translation covers was lacking.
method: The author derives a sufficient condition phrased in terms of the covering geometry and the associated affine/translation structure, then applies it to branched covers of square-tiled surfaces to build explicit examples.
result: New examples of surfaces satisfying the Veech dichotomy that are not Veech surfaces are constructed, extending the known class of dichotomy-holding surfaces beyond the single-branch-point case.
conclusion: The criterion broadens the understanding of which translation surfaces enjoy the Veech dichotomy, showing the property is not confined to Veech surfaces or the previously known branched covers.

title: Memory Safety Isn't All You Need: Code Reuse Attacks In Memory Safe Languages
authors: Musard Balliu Eric Cornelissen
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory safety rules out classical code reuse attacks that rely on arbitrary memory corruption, but does not eliminate code reuse altogether. Attacks such as object injection, prototype pollution, class pollution, DOM clobbering, and DOM script gadgets arise in memory-safe languages without violating the underlying memory safety abstraction. We show that these seemingly different attacks share a common structure: Attacker-controlled data influences accesses to shared runtime state, such as runtime type information, prototype or class state, and the DOM, and a value fetched from that state subsequently influences a security-sensitive operation. Drawing on this insight, we develop a language-agnostic framework that decomposes an attack into a weakness, ending in a fetch from shared runtime state, and a gadget, which propagates the fetched value to a sensitive sink. We show that the framework captures five established attack classes and use it to derive stateless, mutating, and recycling weaknesses, together with simple, vertical, and horizontal gadget structures. We further systematize existing defenses into three common strategies - mediation, minimization, and constraint - and use them to derive candidate defense directions. Finally, we develop a model language that gives a formal account of code-reuse weaknesses and potential conditions for gadgets and end-to-end vulnerabilities.
tldr: This paper analyzes code-reuse attacks in memory-safe languages and proposes a language-agnostic framework for understanding their weaknesses and gadgets.
motivation: Memory safety eliminates classical memory-corruption attacks but does not prevent code reuse via object injection, prototype pollution, class pollution, DOM clobbering, and DOM script gadgets.
method: The authors identify a common structure in these attacks and formalize it as a weakness ending in a fetch from shared runtime state plus a gadget propagating the fetched value to a sensitive sink; they also model a language to formalize code-reuse weaknesses.
result: The framework captures five established attack classes, derives stateless, mutating, and recycling weaknesses along with simple, vertical, and horizontal gadget structures, and systematizes defenses into mediation, minimization, and constraint strategies.
conclusion: Code-reuse attacks remain relevant in memory-safe languages, and the proposed framework provides a foundation for systematizing attacks and deriving defense directions.

title: When The Spec Sheet Lies: Injection Attacks On LLM-Generated Compliance Artifacts
authors: Adriana Watson, Marco B\"ucheler, Grant Richards
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become used more commonly across a variety of fields, a growing body of research has highlighted particular concerns surrounding model security. Notably, prompt injection attacks, where malicious instructions are inserted into prompts, are particularly simple to implement yet capable of inducing devastating effects on the fidelity of model outputs. While there is substantial research surrounding attack models and their effects on chat-based models, browser add-ons, and coding agents, the impact of these same attacks on industrial LLM-generated artifacts has been left largely unexplored. As LLM-enabled agents are increasingly used to skim and generate industrial documents such as Safety Data Sheets (SDS), Quality Control (QC) documents, and Digital Product Passports (DPP), it remains unclear how adversaries may influence these systems to manipulate generated compliance artifacts. This work aims to address this core inquiry by examining how a variety of prompt injection attacks can compromise LLMs with industrial document generation tasks. The study finds that injection attack success varies significantly across different models. Active falsification injections are most successful under all scenarios, while models tend to be most robust against passively injected override requests.
tldr: The paper studies how prompt injection attacks can manipulate LLM-generated industrial compliance documents such as Safety Data Sheets, QC documents, and Digital Product Passports.
motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used to read and generate industrial compliance artifacts, yet the vulnerability of these pipelines to adversarial prompt injection has been largely unexplored compared with chat, browser, and coding-agent settings.
method: The authors systematically test a variety of prompt injection attack types (active falsification, passive override requests, etc.) against multiple LLMs performing industrial document generation tasks.
result: Attack success varies substantially across models; active falsification injections succeed most often in all scenarios, while models are comparatively robust against passively injected override requests.
conclusion: Industrial LLM workflows for compliance documents are vulnerable to adversarial manipulation, motivating model- and pipeline-level defenses for document generation.

title: Spreads Don't Price A Rival Market Maker's Information
authors: Oliver James Oberle, Damien Berriaud, Roger Wattenhofer
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When one market maker becomes better informed, do its competitors widen their bid-ask spreads? Adverse-selection reasoning suggests that they should, because the better-informed maker avoids toxic order flow and leaves more of it to the others, and the closest model of competition with an informed dealer predicts more conservative quotes by the uninformed dealers. We study this question in a stochastic quoting game in which one maker receives a private signal of varying precision about a persistent state that drives order flow. Strategies are learned with independent reinforcement learning, which we benchmark against an exact dynamic-programming solution of the single-agent case. In none of the configurations we examine does the average spread of the uninformed makers increase with the rival's precision. Where competition for order flow is weak, the slope of their spread in precision is statistically equivalent to zero within half an action tick; where competition is strong, their spread tightens. The informed maker's own spread tightens markedly in every configuration and serves as a positive control. These results hold with two, three and four makers, across an eightfold variation in the depth of the background liquidity, with a background quote that reprices after toxic fills, and under price-time priority. Our measurements point to a competitive trade-off. In the model the total toxicity of the flow does not depend on any maker's information. A better-informed maker avoids more of it, and where this leaves more toxic flow to its competitors, it also quotes more tightly, so that a wider quote would cost them more order flow than it would save in adverse selection. The uninformed makers adjust the skew of their quotes and their inventory instead, and the rival's information changes the distribution of profits across makers while quoted spreads remain nearly unchanged.
tldr: A reinforcement-learning agent-based study of whether a market maker's bid-ask spread widens when a competing market maker becomes better informed about order flow.
motivation: Adverse-selection reasoning predicts uninformed market makers should quote more conservatively when a rival holds a private signal, but this has not been tested in a stochastic quoting game with learning agents.
method: The authors model a stochastic quoting game with two to four makers, one receiving a private signal of varying precision about a persistent state driving order flow; strategies are learned via independent reinforcement learning and benchmarked against exact dynamic programming for the single-agent case.
result: Across all configurations, the uninformed makers' average spread never increases with the rival's precision — it is flat where competition is weak and tightens where competition is strong — while the informed maker's own spread always tightens (positive control).
conclusion: Uninformed makers instead adjust quote skew and inventory, so a rival's superior information redistributes profits without materially changing quoted spreads, reflecting a competitive trade-off between order-flow capture and adverse selection.

title: Orbit Ai: Evaluating Tool-Augmented Agents For Enterprise Question Answering
authors: Rishabh Gupta, Uday Kharatmol, Krishna Bhatt, Avadhesh Nagar, Naman Sanotiya, Tarun Jain
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19333v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise information is commonly stored across multiple platforms rather than in one centralized location. Answering questions about workplace activities may require information from several sources, including project documents, task management systems, and team conversations. Therefore, we evaluate Orbit AI, a tool-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system that uses a ReAct agent implemented with LangGraph to retrieve and combine information from three different workspace sources. We compare three configurations: (1) a standalone LLM without retrieval, (2) document-based RAG, and (3) a multi-tool agent with access to all three sources. The held-out evaluation set contains 80 questions designed for Phase 3 workspace; Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite achieves an accuracy of 86.25% with the complete agent. Document-only RAG achieves 60.00% (26.25 pp higher), and the plain LLM achieves 23.13%. For multi-source questions, the full agent answers 84.38%, while document-only RAG answers 40.63%, a 43.75 pp increase. The evaluated Llama 3.2 configuration with local inference achieves 5.50% overall correctness under rubric v2.2. The Llama 3.2 full-agent configuration achieves a held-out accuracy of 52.50%, which is 1.88 pp higher than the accuracy of document-only RAG. The gain of Gemini is equivalent to 26.25 pp. The comparison must be taken with a pinch of salt, because Gemini was accessed via an API hosted by them, while Llama was run locally via Ollama and the models are of different size. It is therefore not possible to isolate the cause of the performance gaps in this experiment. The paper also addresses the constraints of the evaluation such as the small artificial workspace and the similarity of the Q53 problem to a problem in the system prompt.
tldr: Orbit AI is a tool-augmented ReAct/RAG agent evaluated on an 80-question enterprise workspace QA benchmark, comparing a plain LLM, document-only RAG, and a multi-tool agent across three workspace sources.
motivation: Enterprise knowledge is scattered across documents, task trackers, and chat, so answering workplace questions often requires combining evidence from multiple platforms rather than a single corpus.
method: The authors build a LangGraph-based ReAct agent with tools over three workspace sources and compare three configurations (no retrieval, document RAG, full multi-tool agent) using Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite and a locally hosted Llama 3.2 under rubric v2.2.
result: Gemini with the full agent reaches 86.25% accuracy versus 60.00% for document-only RAG and 23.13% for the plain LLM, with the largest gains (84.38% vs 40.63%) on multi-source questions; the local Llama 3.2 runs score 5.50% and 52.50%, but model size and hosting differences prevent isolating the cause.
conclusion: Multi-tool agentic retrieval substantially outperforms single-source RAG on enterprise QA, though the small synthetic workspace, prompt leakage (Q53), and confounded model comparison limit the strength of the claims.

title: Vast: Compiling Grounded Vulnerability Scenarios Into Verifiable, Multi-Step Environments For Evaluating Llm Red-Team Agents
authors: Zhen Wan
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) security agents requires reproducible environments whose workflow difficulty can be varied and whose failures can be diagnosed. We present VAST (Verifiable Adversarial Scenario Training & Evaluation), a declarative range compiler separating vulnerability scenarios from a compiler-introduced workflow-hardening layer. Following a post-hoc code and AST audit across all topics, the main benchmark retains 109 seed edges (45 with strict upstream CVE annotations), 72 family identifiers (62 under shared-HMAC relay grouping), 81 topic configurations (76 core plus 5 bounded execution models), and 1,387 instances (359 canonical four-gate-revalidated specs plus 1,028 seed variants) in a 42:39 partition. On the TopicServer compiler stratum, a budget-matched 270-episode prompt contrast across 10 compiled mechanism-family clusters (30 P2/P3/P4 instances, 40 turns, temperature 0.0) shows that glm-5.3, grok-4.7, and deepseek-v4-pro solve 12/90 instances under contract_only and 14/90 under generic_hint (cluster sign p=1.00), whereas supplying the shared workflow protocol in full_guide lifts completion to 76/90 (28/30, 23/30, 25/30; cluster sign p<=0.00391). On the separate ranges_v2 ledger, a 126-episode evaluation across 6 non-TopicServer workflows and multi-container Docker/Linux stacks solves 88/126 (69.8%) (28/42, 31/42, 29/42), while an 18-episode intervention on asynchronous Redis worker chaining (v2_02) lifts solves from 0/18 to 18/18 (100%) in 4-6 turns when installed worker modules are disclosed in GET /sched/directory. Finally, a three-seed (s in {42, 1024, 2025}) LoRA recipe comparison on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct across 37 lineage-disjoint families (231 episodes on 33 held-out instances) yields 0/33 for Base, 1.67 +/- 2.89 / 33 for Golden SFT, and 4.67 +/- 2.31 / 33 for Header-Recovery SFT, with all solves on v2_03.
tldr: VAST is a declarative compiler that turns grounded vulnerability descriptions into reproducible multi-step Docker-based environments for evaluating LLM red-team agents.
motivation: Evaluating LLM security agents requires reproducible environments with tunable workflow difficulty and diagnosable failures, which existing benchmarks do not provide.
method: The authors build a range compiler separating vulnerability scenarios from a workflow-hardening layer, then run budget-matched prompt-contrast evaluations, an intervention study on Redis worker chaining, and a LoRA fine-tuning comparison on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct.
result: Full workflow disclosure lifts task completion from 12-14/90 to 76/90, the ranges_v2 ledger solves 88/126, the Redis intervention goes from 0/18 to 18/18, and fine-tuning yields at most 4.67/33 solves.
conclusion: Environment scaffolding and protocol disclosure dominate agent performance, while current fine-tuning recipes yield only marginal gains on these cybersecurity tasks.

title: Protecting The System, Stranding The User: The Limits Of Multi-Agent Authorization
authors: Clifford Neuman Gurpriya Bhatia
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Current multi-agent authorization architectures prioritize system integrity over human outcomes. While recent models successfully prevent privilege escalation, they externalize the cost of failure onto the human operator. Re-centering authorization around human impact exposes four structural vulnerabilities in current paradigms. First, calling an agent's understanding of user intent verified is misleading. Intent has no formal definition, so no check against it can be definitive. Systems should instead report an openly probabilistic estimate and scale their caution with the risk of the action. Second, we argue that dynamic trust scores do not survive multi-agent handoffs; transmitting algorithmic judgment across a company boundary without underlying evidence risks violating Contextual Integrity. Third, treating a safely halted workflow as a successful refusal is a category error if it strands the user; compensating actions must be bound directly to the capability token, not only to the planning layer. Finally, we hypothesize that frictionless automated recovery introduces a moral hazard, disincentivizing developers from building robust initial intent checks. We conclude by proposing an architectural synthesis to bridge the gap between deterministic security and human outcomes, alongside the fundamental theoretical limits that remain unresolved.
tldr: The paper argues that current multi-agent authorization architectures protect system integrity at the expense of human users, and proposes re-centering authorization design around human impact.
motivation: Privilege-escalation defenses in multi-agent AI systems externalize failure costs onto human operators, and existing notions such as 'verified intent' and dynamic trust scores are poorly founded.
method: Conceptual and architectural analysis identifying four structural vulnerabilities (ill-defined intent verification, non-transferable trust scores across organizational boundaries, conflating safe halting with successful refusal, and moral hazard from frictionless recovery), followed by a proposed architectural synthesis.
result: No formal theorems or experiments; the paper offers a critique of current paradigms and sketches design principles binding compensating actions to capability tokens and probabilistic intent estimates.
conclusion: Bridging deterministic security guarantees and human outcomes requires architectural changes, and several fundamental theoretical limits remain unresolved.

title: Compositional Exploits In Autonomous Coding Agents: Attack Mechanics And Ephemeral Defense
authors: Nehal Kathrotia Deep Shah
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous coding agents (such as Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenHands) rely on third-party tools to inspect files, run commands, and call external APIs. Today's security auditors evaluate these tools almost entirely in isolation: static linters and AST checkers verify that each individual tool contains no malicious code at installation time. In this paper, we show that isolated tool auditing is fundamentally flawed. We expose compositional exploits in autonomous coding agents, an emergent vulnerability class where an agent chains individually harmless tools to execute an unauthorized attack. Much like code-reuse attacks in binary exploitation, this threat requires no malware; instead, the agent stitches together legitimate tool operations across turns over shared workspace files, environment variables, and chat memory. Across a 560-task benchmark suite (360 exploit tasks across 8 hazard classes and 200 benign developer and cloud workflows), unprotected frontier models (Gemini 3.5, 3.7, and 3.8 Flash) execute compositional exploit chains with a 72.9% to 84.5% success rate, while five leading single-tool pre-distribution scanners exhibit a 0% detection rate across all constituent tools. To eliminate compositional exploits, we present CompGuard, an OS-grounded defense uniting two planes: (1) a Cognitive Control Plane that issues single-skill capability leases and tracks dataflow provenance, and (2) an OS Kernel Enforcement Layer using Linux Landlock LSM v4, seccomp-BPF socket filters, and an ephemeral loopback proxy to close the invocation gap. CompGuard achieves a 100% Defense Block Rate (0.0% to 0.8% pre-teardown Net ASR) at 61.4 microseconds interposition overhead, preserves a 98.0% solve rate on benign developer workflows, and triggers zero false alarms across 615 real cloud diagnostic calls.
tldr: The paper identifies compositional exploits in autonomous coding agents, where individually benign tools are chained into unauthorized attack sequences, and proposes CompGuard, an OS-grounded capability-lease and kernel-enforcement defense.
motivation: Current tool-auditing practice checks third-party tools in isolation, which the authors argue misses emergent vulnerabilities that arise when an agent composes legitimate operations across turns via shared files, environment variables, and chat memory.
method: A 560-task benchmark (360 exploit tasks over 8 hazard classes plus 200 benign workflows) is used to measure exploit success and scanner detection, and CompGuard is introduced combining a Cognitive Control Plane (single-skill capability leases, dataflow provenance) with an OS kernel layer (Landlock LSM v4, seccomp-BPF socket filters, ephemeral loopback proxy).
result: Frontier models execute compositional exploit chains with 72.9%-84.5% success while five leading pre-distribution scanners detect 0%; CompGuard achieves a 100% defense block rate at 61.4 microseconds overhead, retains a 98.0% benign solve rate, and produces zero false alarms over 615 cloud diagnostic calls.
conclusion: Isolated per-tool auditing is fundamentally insufficient for securing autonomous coding agents, and OS-level ephemeral capability enforcement offers a practical, low-overhead remedy.

title: Recovery Gone Too Far: Understanding And Repairing Risky Fallback In Llm Agents
authors: Liwen Wang, Jiangrong Wu, Zongjie Li, Zongyi Lyu, Shuai Wang, Shing-Chi Cheung
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents interact with their environments through tools, reading repositories, running builds, and pushing code. When a tool fails with an ordinary error, such as a rate limit or a timeout, the agent can fall back to a substitute tool and still complete the task. However, the same fallback that completes a task in one environment can cross an action boundary in another. For example, after a push is rejected, a forced push in one repository replaces only the agent's own commits, while in a different repository it also removes another author's commits. We call such a fallback a risky fallback. To understand this phenomenon, we conduct an empirical study on 304 scenarios that span eight domains and cover 55 real CVEs. All four mainstream models we evaluate exhibit risky fallback, with action-boundary violations in up to 96.8% of risky scenarios. We further evaluate three mainstream mitigations and find that none of them is effective against risky fallback. We then present nrepair. At each call to the substitute tool, nrepair scores the agent's context with a monitor whose threshold is calibrated on normal runs alone; when the monitor triggers, it withholds the call once and returns the decision to the agent. nrepair reduces action-boundary violations on all four models, by up to 76.0% (from 67.5% to 16.2%), at a negligible runtime cost. On most models, the normal success rate drops by less than 7%. We also evaluate nrepair on two production agents, Claude Code and Codex, and find that it is equally effective on both.
tldr: An empirical and mitigation study of 'risky fallback' behavior in LLM agents, where a substitute tool used after an ordinary error violates action boundaries, plus a runtime monitor called nrepair that withholds such calls.
motivation: LLM agents routinely fall back to alternative tools after benign failures like rate limits or timeouts, but the same fallback can be destructive in a different environment (e.g., a forced push deleting another author's commits), and no existing mitigation handles this failure mode.
method: The authors build 304 scenarios across eight domains covering 55 real CVEs, test four mainstream models, evaluate three existing mitigations, and propose nrepair, which scores agent context with a monitor threshold calibrated only on normal runs and withholds a triggering call once, returning the decision to the agent.
result: All four models exhibit risky fallback with action-boundary violations in up to 96.8% of risky scenarios; existing mitigations fail. nrepair reduces violations by up to 76.0% (67.5% to 16.2%) with negligible runtime cost and under 7% normal-success loss, and is effective on Claude Code and Codex.
conclusion: Risky fallback is a widespread, previously unmitigated safety problem in LLM agents, and a lightweight calibrated monitor can substantially reduce boundary violations without meaningfully hurting task success.

title: Discovering Programmatic Policies From Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Controllers
authors: Lindong Xie, Yang Zhang, Beiyu Song, Zeren Xing, Flora D. Salim, Edward Chung
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traffic signal control (TSC) is critical for mitigating urban congestion. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved strong performance by learning adaptive policies from traffic observations, but learned neural controllers are often opaque, structurally complex, and difficult to generalize across scenarios. We propose PPL-TSC, a programmatic policy learning framework that distills compact and human-readable TSC policies from DRL teachers. PPL-TSC formulates policy learning as an evolutionary search over phase utility functions (PUFs), which score candidate signal phases and select the highest-utility phase for execution. Each generation consists of four steps: policy generation, policy review, policy calibration, and policy evaluation. In the generation step, a large language model (LLM) acts as a semantics-aware evolutionary operator to propose and refine candidate PUFs. Generated PUFs are screened through explicit checks for syntactic validity, mathematical soundness, and consistency with TSC principles, with invalid ones repaired through iterative feedback. Valid PUFs are then calibrated to improve behavioral fidelity to the DRL teacher, and evaluated using a joint score combining teacher fidelity and traffic-control performance to select candidates for the next generation. Extensive experiments across diverse traffic scenarios and representative DRL-based controllers show that PPL-TSC produces compact and human-readable policies, achieves competitive performance for most teacher families, improves transfer generalization, and substantially reduces computational cost. Code is available at [URL].
tldr: PPL-TSC distills compact, human-readable programmatic traffic-signal-control policies from deep reinforcement learning teachers using an LLM-driven evolutionary search over phase utility functions.
motivation: DRL-based traffic signal controllers perform well but are opaque, structurally complex, and generalize poorly across scenarios, motivating interpretable and transferable policy representations.
method: Policy learning is cast as evolutionary search over phase utility functions, with an LLM acting as a semantics-aware evolutionary operator proposing and refining candidates, followed by syntactic/mathematical review, fidelity calibration to the DRL teacher, and joint evaluation of teacher fidelity plus traffic performance.
result: Across diverse traffic scenarios and representative DRL controllers, the framework produces compact readable policies with competitive performance for most teacher families, improved transfer generalization, and substantially lower computational cost.
conclusion: LLM-guided programmatic distillation offers a practical route to interpretable, transferable traffic signal control policies derived from black-box RL teachers.

title: Planar PArcK Is PSPACE-complete
authors: Kanae Yoshiwatari Craig Tennenhouse
abstract: ArXiv:2611.20138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Partizan Arc Kayles, or PArcK, is a partizan combinatorial game on edge colored graphs, and is a generalization of the game Domineering. Previously, PArcK was shown to be PSPACE-complete on bipartite graphs. In this paper we show that PArcK is PSPACE-complete even when restricted to planar graphs of degree at most three by a reduction from Generalized Hex.
tldr: Planar Partizan Arc Kayles (PArcK) is proven PSPACE-complete even on planar graphs of maximum degree three via a reduction from Generalized Hex.
motivation: PArcK was previously known to be PSPACE-complete only on bipartite graphs; the authors aim to sharpen the complexity classification by restricting the graph class to planar, low-degree instances.
method: A reduction from the PSPACE-complete game Generalized Hex to PArcK on planar graphs of degree at most three, carefully constructing edge-colored gadgets that simulate the Hex board.
result: PArcK remains PSPACE-complete under the strong restriction to planar graphs with maximum degree three, strengthening earlier bipartite-graph hardness.
conclusion: The intractability of PArcK is robust to severe structural restrictions, extending the landscape of PSPACE-complete partizan combinatorial games.

title: Paying Creators For Training Data Can Increase Ai Displacement
authors: Lijuan Luo, Emaad Manzoor, Nathan Yang, Fan Yao
abstract: ArXiv:2611.20204v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative AI increasingly competes with creators while using their content as training data. In response, policymakers have called for platforms to compensate creators for training data use and allow opting out. We study how such policies affect creator displacement in a model of a platform where creators choose whether to contribute training data and consumers choose between purchasing from creators and prompting generative AI trained on their content. When compensation is required, the low-quality creator chooses to remain solely as a training data supplier while AI fully displaces her demand, despite AI quality and the price the platform charges for AI-generated content being identical with and without compensation. Without compensation, the risk of losing creators and their training data constrains the platform to set the price of creators' content to preserve their demand. This constraint also prevents further AI displacement as AI improves, with the platform raising AI prices while keeping creators' prices and demand unchanged to prevent exit. Compensation increases creators' payoffs and total surplus but reduces consumer surplus. Our findings highlight how compensation policies for training data can shape creators' economic roles in a future with more capable generative AI.
tldr: A platform-economics model showing that mandatory compensation for creators' training data can accelerate AI-driven displacement of low-quality creators while raising creator payoffs and total surplus at the expense of consumer surplus.
motivation: Policymakers have proposed compensating creators whose content trains generative AI and allowing opt-outs, but the market consequences of such policies for creator displacement are unclear.
method: The authors build a stylized model of a platform where creators decide whether to supply training data and consumers choose between buying from creators or prompting generative AI trained on that content, comparing regimes with and without required compensation.
result: Under compensation, low-quality creators become pure data suppliers and are fully displaced by AI even though AI quality and AI pricing are unchanged; without compensation, the platform must suppress AI displacement to retain creators and their data.
conclusion: Compensation policies reshape creators' economic roles as AI capabilities grow, increasing creator welfare and total surplus but reducing consumer surplus.

title: History Independence And Base-dominant Rigidity For Polynomial Skew Products
authors: Yan Mary He
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study history independence of fast directions and its relation to the Binder--DeMarco dimension formula for regular polynomial skew products of degree [MATH]. Assuming uniform expansion on the support of the measure of maximal entropy and a base Lyapunov exponent larger than the vertical exponent, we prove that history independence is equivalent to conjugacy to a polynomial product by an affine shear map. Under history independence, the measure of maximal entropy satisfies the Binder--DeMarco dimension formula. If, in addition, the splitting is dominated, the dimension formula also implies history independence. The proof first upgrades the measurable fast direction to a holomorphic line field and then uses its invariance on periodic fibers to force the affine product structure. The converse dimension implication combines an entropy comparison argument with rigidity of local symmetries of periodic fiber Julia sets.
tldr: The paper studies history independence for regular polynomial skew products and relates it to the Binder--DeMarco dimension formula and affine product rigidity.
motivation: The work aims to characterize when fast directions in polynomial skew product dynamics are history independent and when this implies or follows from dimension formulas for measures of maximal entropy.
method: Under uniform expansion and a base Lyapunov exponent dominance condition, the proof upgrades measurable fast directions to holomorphic line fields and uses invariance on periodic fibers, entropy comparison, and local symmetry rigidity.
result: History independence is shown equivalent to conjugacy to a polynomial product by an affine shear map, and under this condition the measure of maximal entropy satisfies the Binder--DeMarco dimension formula; dominated splitting gives a converse implication.
conclusion: The paper establishes rigidity and dimension-formula connections for polynomial skew products, but it is a pure complex-dynamics result with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Compromise Optimization Over Incompatible Efficient Sets Using A Minimax Distance Approach With Polyhedral Characterization And An Application To Fisheries Management
authors: Mustapha Kaci
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The efficient sets associated with different decision-makers may have an empty intersection, even when their objectives are linear and the common feasible region is a compact polytope. In this paper, we consider a compromise criterion that minimizes the largest weighted distance from a feasible decision to the respective efficient sets of the decision-makers. First, we establish the existence of an optimal compromise and show that the formulation recovers the common efficient set whenever it is nonempty. We then derive a lower bound based on the separation of efficient sets and obtain an exact formulation in terms of finitely many linear programs by exploiting their polyhedral structure. Next, we examine the effect of approximating the efficient sets and establish a stability bound expressed in terms of the Hausdorff distance. Finally, we illustrate the applicability of the proposed approach through a numerical study of harvest allocation between two interconnected fishing zones.
tldr: The paper proposes a minimax-distance compromise criterion for reconciling incompatible efficient sets of multiple decision-makers, with polyhedral linear-programming formulations demonstrated on a fisheries harvest allocation problem.
motivation: Efficient sets of different decision-makers can be disjoint even under linear objectives over a common compact polytope, so a principled compromise selection rule is needed.
method: The authors minimize the largest weighted distance to each decision-maker's efficient set, prove existence of an optimal compromise, derive a separation-based lower bound, and obtain an exact reformulation as finitely many linear programs exploiting polyhedral structure; stability under approximation is bounded via Hausdorff distance.
result: The formulation recovers the common efficient set when nonempty, yields exact LP-based computation, and provides a stability bound; a numerical study of harvest allocation between two interconnected fishing zones illustrates it.
conclusion: The approach offers a tractable, provably stable compromise mechanism for conflicting multiobjective decision problems, with fisheries management as a practical case.

title: Zero Area Of Quartic Fibonacci Julia Sets
authors: Runze Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18993v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a computer-assisted proof that the Julia set of the degree-four Fibonacci renormalization 2-periodic point has zero planar Lebesgue measure. As a corollary, the degree four Fibonacci polynomial [MATH] has zero measure Julia set.
tldr: The paper provides a computer-assisted proof that the Julia set of the degree-four Fibonacci renormalization 2-periodic point has zero planar Lebesgue measure.
motivation: The work addresses a problem in complex dynamics concerning the measure of Julia sets for Fibonacci renormalization points, a topic unrelated to quantum information science.
method: The author uses computer-assisted proof techniques to establish the zero measure property for a specific degree-four Fibonacci polynomial.
result: The main result is that the Julia set of the degree-four Fibonacci renormalization 2-periodic point has zero planar Lebesgue measure, with a corollary for the degree-four Fibonacci polynomial.
conclusion: This is a mathematical result in holomorphic dynamics with no apparent connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: We Have All The Cards: Securing Agent Cards At The Operational Trust Boundary Of The Agent2Agent Protocol
authors: Miguel A. Guirao Aguilera, Satyajayant Misra, Efren Lopez-Morales
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agent interoperability protocols enable orchestrators to discover and invoke external agents using machine-readable metadata. In the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, Agent Cards contain attacker-controllable natural-language fields that may influence agent selection before a provider is invoked, creating a pre-invocation trust problem. We characterize this discovery-time attack surface through a taxonomy of ten Agent Card manipulation attacks and present SECCARD, a layered validation framework combining protocol checks, deterministic analysis, and LLM-based semantic reasoning. We measure the emerging public A2A ecosystem by probing 36.1 million Internet domains and collecting 310 deployed Agent Cards. Two annotators independently label the corpus with 96.8% agreement. We then construct a 660-card real-card perturbation benchmark with matched benign controls and a 260-card synthetic adversarial benchmark spanning all ten attack categories. On controlled attacks injected into real Agent Cards, the strongest semantic judge achieves 97.0% security recall at a 1.7% false-positive rate. Across nine LLM judges on the synthetic benchmark, security recall ranges from 25.8% to 92.3%, demonstrating substantial model-dependent variation. These results show that SECCARD effectively identifies Agent Card manipulations spanning all ten discovery-time attack classes while preserving benign Agent Cards, but also reveal that its effectiveness depends critically on the choice of the underlying LLM judge.
tldr: The paper characterizes discovery-time attack surfaces in the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol's Agent Cards and proposes SECCARD, a layered validation framework combining protocol checks, deterministic analysis, and LLM-based semantic judging.
motivation: Agent Cards in the A2A protocol contain attacker-controllable natural-language fields that can influence orchestrator agent selection before any provider is invoked, creating a pre-invocation trust problem not addressed by existing security mechanisms.
method: The authors build a taxonomy of ten Agent Card manipulation attacks, probe 36.1 million Internet domains to collect 310 deployed Agent Cards, and construct a 660-card real-card perturbation benchmark plus a 260-card synthetic adversarial benchmark to evaluate SECCARD and nine LLM judges.
result: The strongest semantic judge achieves 97.0% security recall at a 1.7% false-positive rate on controlled attacks, while security recall across nine LLM judges on the synthetic benchmark varies widely from 25.8% to 92.3%.
conclusion: SECCARD effectively detects Agent Card manipulations across all ten attack classes while preserving benign cards, but its effectiveness depends critically on the choice of the underlying LLM judge.

title: Optional Traps: An Empirical Study Of Llm Agents Against Credential Deception And Alert-Driven Revocation
authors: Raditio Ghifiardi
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deception (honeypots, decoys and canary credentials) rests on a simple premise: legitimate users never touch a fake asset, so any touch is a high-confidence signal. We ask whether that premise holds when the attacker is a large language model (LLM) agent, and what deception contributes once ordinary hardening is in place. We built an isolated, hash-chained lab around a mock Records API and report four studies. (1) In an exploratory run, a local 9.7B-parameter model ignored every optional decoy, read a genuinely leaked service key from a debug endpoint and exported the protected records in both static and adaptive deception modes. (2) After removing the leak, planting a canary credential in its place and revoking the offending client, a frozen 60-session study with a 4B-parameter model found export success of 20/20 at baseline, 0/20 with hardening alone and 0/20 with hardening plus deception (exact paired McNemar p = 1.9e-6 baseline vs. defended; p = 1 hardened vs. defended). Deception added detection and per-client revocation in 19 of 20 defended sessions, but no measurable prevention beyond hardening. (3) On Google Cloud, a real OpenCanary login alert was authenticated, signed and turned into revocation of the attacking client; the first denied export followed within an observed upper bound of 303 ms, a separate legitimate client completed 100/100 requests, and all 14 control checks passed. (4) In multi-agent swarm engagements, agents that used the canary were revoked 39-59 s after the bait was served without affecting siblings, but one model-driven legitimate agent also took the bait, a false-positive risk specific to LLM clients. Against LLM agents, traps must sit on the attacker's path rather than beside it, closing real weaknesses does the preventive work, and deception's measurable value is fast, attributable detection. All results are lab-scale and are not a production claim.
tldr: This paper empirically studies whether deception such as honeypots, decoys, and canary credentials is effective against LLM agents, and how much deception adds beyond ordinary security hardening.
motivation: The authors test the common security premise that touching a fake asset is a high-confidence attack signal, specifically when the attacker is an LLM agent rather than a human.
method: They build an isolated hash-chained lab around a mock Records API and run four studies involving local LLM agents, canary credentials, revocation, Google Cloud OpenCanary alerts, and multi-agent swarm engagements.
result: Hardening alone prevented export in the frozen 60-session study, while deception added detection and revocation but no measurable prevention beyond hardening; traps on the attacker's path were necessary, and false positives occurred when a legitimate LLM agent touched the bait.
conclusion: Against LLM agents, security traps should be placed on the attacker's actual path, real vulnerability closure provides the preventive value, and deception's measurable contribution is fast attributable detection rather than prevention.

title: Security Authentication As Protective Friction: Understanding The Dual Effects Of Authentication Measures In e-Government Platform
authors: Jianshan Pan, Zongyi Chen, Qiyou Lin, Xiaofang Cai
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: E-Government platforms, such as government credit platforms, handle highly sensitive personal data, requiring stringent security authentication (e.g., facial recognition, multi-factor verification) that protects users but impedes their experience. Drawing on Tomalin's (2023) e-friction typology and the emerging literature on beneficial design friction, we reconceptualize these authentication measures as protective friction, a theoretically distinct form of non-elective, overt, impeding e-friction that serves a security-enhancing function. We propose a dual-pathway model in which protective friction simultaneously reduces privacy-security risk perception (protection pathway) and increases effort cost (cost pathway), with self-efficacy moderating only the risk pathway. This differential pattern suggests that what matters is not users' ability to overcome friction, but their comprehension of its protective purpose, a construct we term protective mechanism comprehension. We outline a mixed-methods research design combining a survey of platform users and semi-structured interviews with platform staff at a Chinese municipal credit center to test this model. This research-in-progress contributes to IS theory by extending e-friction research from conceptual typology to empirical investigation, identifying when security friction becomes beneficial rather than burdensome.
tldr: This information-systems research-in-progress reconceptualizes e-government security authentication (facial recognition, multi-factor verification) as 'protective friction' and proposes a dual-pathway model linking it to privacy-security risk perception and effort cost.
motivation: E-government credit platforms handle sensitive personal data and require stringent authentication that protects users while degrading their experience; existing e-friction typologies are conceptual and lack empirical testing of when friction is beneficial.
method: A mixed-methods design combining a survey of platform users with semi-structured interviews of staff at a Chinese municipal credit center, testing a dual-pathway model with self-efficacy as a moderator of the risk pathway only.
result: No empirical results yet reported; the paper is research-in-progress presenting the theoretical model, hypotheses, and planned study design.
conclusion: The authors argue that what matters is users' comprehension of friction's protective purpose ('protective mechanism comprehension') rather than their ability to overcome friction, extending e-friction research from typology to empirical investigation.

title: CoSyDelay: Cognitive Symbolic Regression For Traffic Delay Estimation
authors: Lindong Xie, Xiexin Zou, Yang Zhang, Beiyu Song, Zeren Xing, Edward Chung
abstract: ArXiv:2611.19946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trustworthy estimation of traffic delays at signalized intersections is critical for modern transportation systems, as it supports proactive traffic control for congestion mitigation. Existing analytical methods often rely on idealized assumptions that limit their accuracy under complex traffic conditions, whereas data-driven methods may achieve strong estimation performance but usually lack transparent structures, which reduces confidence in their practical application. To address these limitations, we propose CoSyDelay, a cognitive symbolic regression (SR) framework for automatically deriving explicit and physically consistent empirical delay estimation expressions (DEEs). Specifically, CoSyDelay decomposes intersection-level delay estimation into turning-movement-level subproblems, thereby reducing the complexity of the symbolic search. During DEE learning, CoSyDelay constructs domain-informed symbolic inputs from traffic variables. Large language models (LLMs) are employed as symbolic search operators to iteratively generate and refine candidate expression structures, whose movement-specific coefficients are subsequently calibrated using approach-level delay labels. A composite fitness function evaluates the learned DEEs jointly in terms of estimation accuracy and compliance with specified traffic-delay principles. Experimental results on multiple signalized intersections demonstrate that the resulting expressions achieve competitive estimation performance while maintaining physical consistency, thereby supporting trustworthy delay estimation. Source code and datasets are available at [URL].
tldr: CoSyDelay is a cognitive symbolic regression framework that uses LLMs as symbolic search operators to derive explicit, physically consistent delay estimation expressions for signalized intersections.
motivation: Trustworthy traffic delay estimation at signalized intersections supports proactive congestion control, but analytical models rely on idealized assumptions while data-driven models lack transparency.
method: The framework decomposes intersection-level delay estimation into turning-movement subproblems, builds domain-informed symbolic inputs, and uses LLMs to iteratively generate and refine candidate expression structures, with coefficients calibrated on approach-level delay labels and a composite fitness function enforcing accuracy and traffic-delay principles.
result: Experiments on multiple signalized intersections show the learned expressions achieve competitive estimation accuracy while maintaining physical consistency.
conclusion: Symbolic regression guided by LLMs yields interpretable, trustworthy delay estimation models, though the work is confined to transportation engineering.

title: Minimality Of The Double Kite Among Strict Two-Pole Configurations Of Unit Triangles
authors: Mike Winkler
abstract: ArXiv:2611.18742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A strict unit-triangle configuration is a finite connected family of closed equilateral unit triangles in which distinct triangles are disjoint or meet at a common vertex, and no vertex belongs to more than two triangles. A vertex belonging to exactly one triangle is a pole. We prove that every strict configuration with one or two poles contains at least fourteen triangles, a sharp bound for two poles attained by the double kite and the reverse double kite. A strict four-regular configuration whose contact graph has an edge cut of size at most two contains at least twenty-eight triangles. A decomposition into three strict two-pole components requires forty-two triangles; both known ring constructions attain the bound.
